speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of National Defence for Air if he is yet in a position to tell the house anything respecting the special inquiry concerning the eastern passage aerodrome. I believe the inquiry was made about six months ago.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. G. POWER (Minister of National Defence for Air):
speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DARTMOUTH, N.S., AIRPORT EASTERN PASSAGE AERODROME CONTRACTS- TILLEY REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not in a position to submit a report to the house, because I have not yet received any. However, in view of the numerous questions which have been addressed to me with respect to this matter, perhaps I had better tell the house what it is all about, without going into any discussion of questions which might be controversial.
There were two main contracts for the development of an aerodrome at Dartmouth, N.S., known as the eastern passage aerodrome. The first of these, for excavation and grading, was dated June 22, 1938, and the second for shaping, surfacing and drainage of runways and gravelling of shoulders was dated, originally, October 6, 1939, but was later rescinded by a revised contract dated January 25, 1940.
The former of these contracts, namely, the one for excavation and grading, was a unit price contract awarded to the lowest bidder after a call for tenders, but the second, for shaping and surfacing, is a cost plus a fixed fee contract awarded to the contractor who had made the lowest bid for grading and was already on the job.
In both cases the requirements of service operations necessitated a great deal more work being done under these contracts than it was contemplated would be necessary when they were made. In other words, the whole development has had to be on a much larger scale.
I believe it is fair to say that there has been no criticism of the quality of the work performed under these contracts or any suggestion that it was not done as expeditiously as possible. At the same time, it has been suggested-at least informally-that the contracts themselves were not all they should have been and that there had been irregularities in connection with them. I believe it has been stated in the press that there are affidavits of a sensational nature made by a former engineer, although I have never seen them.
At all events, it did appear that a full inquiry should be made and, as a number of departments are involved-the departments of Munitions and Supply, National Defence, National Defence for Air and, to some extent, the Department of Finance-I determined last October to ask one of the leading members of the Canadian bar to make such an inquiry. He is doing so now. The fact that a man of Mr. Tilley's experience has taken several months to complete his inquiry indicates, I believe, that the questions involved were of a nature not to have been dealt with as a matter of routine by departmental officials already overburdened. Mr. Tilley advised us a short time ago that he wished to make a personal

Royal Canadian Navy
visit to the aerodrome. I have since been advised he has made such a visit to the aerodrome at Halifax. And I have been advised by telephone that there is every expectation that he will make his report within a few days.

subtopic: EDITORIAL COMMENT ON PRECEDENCE OF SENIOR OFFICERS WHILE IN PORT

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Hon. ANGUS L. MACDONALD (Minister of National Defence for Naval Services): Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to an editorial appearing in to-day's issue of the Globe and Mail of Toronto, entitled "Ridiculous Pomposity." The editorial is rather lengthy, and I shall not endeavour to read all of it. However, I shall place before the house the more important parts. It begins thus:
There is a far Canadian city which has been deprived of its name. It is now known as "An eastern Canadian port." The population of this city knows that Canada is at war. Its harbour is full of ships one day and almost deserted the next. It is the seat of Canada's naval power, and it is in this port that the Rear-Admiral commanding the Canadian navy flies his flag.
There is another admiral in that port. He is there actually, not theoretically. He commands a British battle squadron, which includes some very powerful units of the Royal Navy operating in the north Atlantic. Because he may not infringe upon the dignities and prerogatives of the newly created Rear-Admiral commanding the newly expanded Canadian navy, the British admiral may not establish a suitable headquarters ashore. Instead, he is obliged to operate from a small vessel which is just removed from the wharf by the interposition of a hulk with gangplanks stretched across it.
Thus propriety, etiquette and prerogative are preserved, and no challenge is made to the authority of the Canadian Rear-Admiral.
Rear-Admiral Bonham Carter, C.V.O., D.S.O., R.N., is the man who is primarily responsible for keeping open the sea lanes of the Atlantic. Canada owes it to him and the men under his command that two divisions of Canadian troops were transported to the British isles without casualty. The admiral himself is not the sort of man who cares very much whether he flies his flag in the eastern Canadian port or whether he is comfortably billeted. But it does seem a little unfortunate that the commander of a British battle squadron should in any way be inconvenienced or circumscribed by reason of the presence of an equal width of new gold braid around another pair of sleeves.
Then-I omit some paragraphs which are not relevant-it continues:
But, because two admirals cannot fly their flags in the same port, the commander-in-chief of the British battle squadron must stay at sea, so that the authority of the Canadian admiral shall be unchallenged.
I would like to say in the first place that the editorial is basically inaccurate, because the Rear Admiral of the Royal Canadian Navy does not fly his flag in Halifax. The Royal Canadian Naval establishment in Halifax is commanded by a commodore of the Royal Canadian Navy, who flies his broad pendant ait his majesty's dockyard there. In the second place, with reference to the 'newly created Rear Admiral commanding the newly expanded Canadian navy" the Canadian Rear Admiral is senior in date of appointment to the British Rear Admiral at Halifax. In the third place, it is a traditional principle of the admiralty that an officer in command of a seagoing force should fly his flag afloat, and there is no case known to me or to my staff of an exception to that rule, apart from a short period at the beginning of the war when the British Rear Admiral at Halifax flew his flag ashore until it was possible to acquire a floating headquarters, now known as His Majesty's Ship Seaborne.
Furthermore, the present position is perfectly well understood by all concerned. The British Rear Admiral at Halifax, the commanding officer on the Atlantic coast, the naval staff here, have all maintained continuously the closest cooperation and harmony. Rear Admiral Bonham Carter has his headquarters on a ship, which it is true is moored to a dock in Halifax, but he has a house in the city where he lives with his wife and children when off duty.
Rear Admiral Bonham Carter is a most gallant and genial gentleman, universally esteemed and liked, and I am sure that no one will be more annoyed and displeased than he at this inaccurate and unnecessary publicity.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is the position with respect to quasi-cooperatives? What is the position? Are they true cooperatives? The law, as I understand it, is that true cooperatives do not pay income tax. What is the position with regard to those which are in the in-between class, such as I suggest, and is there any reason why they should not pay income tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
One would have to take
individual instances and determine whether any particular cooperative or alleged cooperative was within the section exempting cooperatives. That is sometimes pretty difficult. I do not think there is very much more to be said about it than that. Apparently the section is fairly clear, but, like many clear sections, when it comes to applying it to a particular group of individuals and the business they are transacting it is often very difficult to know whether a concern is a cooperative within the meaning of the act, and important disputes have arisen as to whether certain business organizations are or are not within the exemption.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The definition is found in part II, section 4, of the

(p) The income of farmers', dairymen's, live-stockmen's, fruit growers', poultrymen's, fishermen's and other like cooperative companies and associations, whether with or without share capital, organized and operated on a cooperative basis, . . .

I had in mind the pools and grain growers of the west. Has an investigation been made into their status, and has it been legally determined that they come within the exemption?

speechtext: The business affairs of the pools are under active investigation at the present time. It has not been definitely determined whether they are subject to income tax or not.

If the
matter is under investigation, that is enough for me.

Paragraph 2 of the resolution deals with investment income. Will the minister explain what changes it is intended to make in the law relating to taxation on investment income, in relation to personal income tax and corporation income tax and also with regard to the tax on non-residents? I think that these points might very well be cleared up at this stage.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is a difficult matter to explain.
I do not know what hon. members have to talk about, but we simply cannot hear what is going on.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
At the present time there is what is called a tax on investment income, but it is not a true tax on investment income except within a very small range, because all income over $14,000 is deemed to be investment income. For instance if a $50,000 salary is the only income of an individual, the part of it over $14,000 is deemed to be investment income. The so-called investment income tax, therefore, is not a true investment income tax. Now there has been an alteration in the rates and schedules, so that there will be on all investment income, over a small exemption at the lower end, a surtax, and the schedules and

Income War Tax Act
rates of taxation in reference to non-investment income have been so framed as virtually to absorb the old graduated so-called investment income tax rates. There is also a flat four per cent tax on investment income in addition to the ordinary graduated income tax.

Does that mean that a person with a taxable income of say $1,000 would pay the income tax rate on that and in addition would pay four per cent on any portion of that income of $1,000 which is derived from dividends, interest, rents or royalties?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

If the $1,000 is over the

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: They have no investment income tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Is he in addition to be charged four per cent under the investment income tax provision, making the total nineteen per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

It would be possible for example for a non-resident to have no net income; nevertheless he would have deducted at the source here in Canada fifteen per cent of the gross amount received. What is
the theory of this change? Is it that it will produce more revenue?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The theory is that a person who is dependent on earned income is not in as stable or solid a position as a person who is dependent to some or to the full extent upon investment income. When he has capital upon which he is deriving an investment income, his future is provided for, so long as he can hold on to his capital. A person who is dependent upon earned income is not in that position, so that it is considered fair to tax investment income at a slightly higher rate than non-investment income.

There has always been
a surtax on that, anyway.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is what I explained a few minutes ago. Under the existing law it has been largely nominal. There has been a surtax which has been called an investment income surtax, but it was applied on salaries as well as on investment income over and above $14,000. In a very large range there was no distinction whatever; it has been a so-called, an alleged, investment income surtax. I am told that $200 or thereabouts is the largest amount by which one person's income tax can exceed another's on the same income by virtue of that surtax.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
That is
a remarkable statement. I refer hon. members to page 52 of the office consolidation of the Income War Tax Act, September, 1940, wherein is set forth "Rates of tax applicable to all persons other than corporations and joint stock companies, in respect of 'investment income'." On an income exceeding $100,000, but not exceeding $150,000, they pay a rate of eight per cent. That does not jibe with what the minister said.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I should
like it demonstrated.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Because

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It may work out that way; I don't know.

As I understand it, before this change was made investment income was taxed only if the amount was $5,000 or over. Now, by this change, you are taxing any sum that is liable to ordinary income tax. In other words if a man dies leaving his widow assets from which she will have an income of $1,750 per year, when she comes to pay income tax she will receive an exemption of $750. On the remaining $1,000 she will pay $150 under the new scale, plus an additional $40 under this investment income tax. Is that the situation? speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think that is quite correct, but I shall answer more fully in a moment.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

I do not want to answer finally, however, because I am under the impression that there is an exemption of a little more than the $750 for investment income. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: This is a very sharp increase.
Will the minister explain the changes that are being made here; and will he also tell us whether or not the present exemptions are to be continued?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: These increases are proposed in view of the provisions of the succession duties resolution. Gifts made within three years before the decease of the decedent are considered as property passing on the death; but gifts made before that time, if they are not made in contemplation of death-that is, if they are not in the category of donatio mortis causa-are not taxable. These gift rates are imposed with a view to discouraging the making of such gifts, having in mind the succession duties.
The rate has been increased considerably.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Are the exemptions to be changed? As I understand it, there is an exemption of $4,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The exemptions are not to be changed. There is one change in connection with the exemptions, but it has no relation to the amount.

That is, the recognized
exemptions are not to be changed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
Then what is the change referred to in the resolution, that section 88(8) (e) be repealed? Why is that paragraph being repealed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The explanation is that
in the case of a gift by a husband to a wife, the husband had been taxed on his income just as though the gift had not been made, and for that reason the gift tax did not apply in such cases. But now, in view of the fact that we are passing a succession duty act, the gift may be made for another purpose. It may be an advantage for a husband to make a gift to his wife for the purpose of avoidance of succession duty.
Can you not get it, then, under your succession duty provisions?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, it might be made at a time when it would not be subject to succession duty, that is, more than three years before the death of the decedent; and for that reason it is proposed to impose a gift tax on that gift.

This really means that you are going to tax by way of income tax the person making this gift; he is to continue paying income tax on that transfer- in other words, it is not to be recognized under the income tax law, but at the same time you are going to tax him under the gift tax provision. You tax him twice.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
And if
he dies within three years you hook him a third time. It is most unfair.
Of course he is not there to hook, then.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Well, the money is. Perhaps his wife is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The gift tax is credited
against the succession duty. That will be a provision of the succession duty act.

I suggest it is hardly fair to repeal that clause. You are already taxing that same amount, the amount of the gift, under section 32 of the Income War Tax Act. You can get that tax now; and in addition, under this proposed amendment, you are going to make him pay a gift tax; if the amount is up to 85,000, you make him pay a gift tax of seven per cent. It is double taxation. I submit that it is not fair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should think there would be a disposition to give a lot away if there were not some safeguard there.

4.	That the rates of national defence tax be increased from 2 per centum to 5 per centum wherever 2 per centum is mentioned and from 3 per centum to 7 per centum wherever 3 per centum is mentioned, and that these rates be effective from the first day of July, 1941.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I tell the minister right now that I am going to oppose this provision for an increase. It is not fair to those in the lower income brackets. The national defence tax is being more than doubled; and in addition to that, you have taken from the wage earner, voluntarily if you will, though in many cases questionably, substantial contributions to war savings certificates. There are other taxes exigible under

the lower income tax range. On top of that, there is the increase in the cost of living which people who are in receipt of wages and income have to pay. Many of those now in receipt of wages or low-rate salaries for a long time did not have steady jobs; they find themselves in the position, perhaps for the first time in many years, of receiving a pay envelope every Saturday night. I suggest that the national defence tax at the old rate is a proper contribution for anybody to make, but to seek to raise the large sum of money which this impost will produce at the increased rates is not fair to people who can least afford to pay. I know the argument is that it is to take their surplus earnings so that they will not squander them on luxuries. Theoretically that is very good; it sounds very well; it will help to prevent inflation. But the tax attaches to people who for the first time in a long period of years are in receipt of a living wage and an assured income. They must have accumulations of debt, unpaid rent, and what not, and the tax should not be raised, at all events for this year. I never objected to the old tax. What I thought was that there would be a large sum of money raised, and that it was a tax which had come to stay in our lifetime. But to increase it to this high level is, in my view, unjust to those in the lower income brackets and I am opposed to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are confronted with a problem here, and we all have a certain amount of responsibility. The hon. gentleman attacked us last year because the tax was too heavy.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Not this one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, not this one, but the income tax on the medium incomes. He said this year that he regarded it as very heavy last year and very heavy this year. Now I suppose he would not suggest a higher income tax on medium incomes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I am not under cross-examination. The minister is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
All right; I will not ask for any answers to my questions, but just the same, I am going to ask the questions and then proceed, so that other hon. members can search their own hearts and say what their answers would be were they in the government's position.
This increase will yield about $80,000,000. It does not apply only to the small income people; it applies to all the taxpayers in Canada, everybody who is receiving an income

Income War Tax Act
of any kind. It is an additional income tax, and it has been taken into account in the fixing of the graduated income tax. It is more or less assimilated to the income tax system of the country. If the suggestion of the hon. gentleman, that we should drop that
S80,000,000, were adopted, our proposed receipts in the year would be reduced from $300,000,000 to about $220,000,000. That would make a tremendous difference; and under these circumstances it is not good enough for an hon. member, whether he be a member of the opposition or not, simply to say that he opposes a particular tax. He must face up to the situation and decide whether he is in favour of getting the amount of taxation we have set out to get, and if he proposes to throw out $80,000,000 of taxes he should suggest some other way of raising the money. There are other ways in which we can raise this amount. We could raise the sales tax from eight to ten per cent and pick up something like $50,000,000-$47,000,000. That was all considered.

It would fall on the same
people.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Not exactly. But this is a
fairer tax than the sales tax, because it applies to income. Nobody pays anything under the national defence tax unless he is in receipt of an income, and then he pays five or seven per cent. If we increased the sales tax and took in about $50,000,000 in that way, to begin with the consumer would be paying considerably more than that. I cannot make an estimate of just what it would be, but I should say at least $60,000,000 or $70,000,000; some people estimate that the loss in pyramiding would be very much greater, and the tax would be paid by a great many people in this country who have not much income at all. It would also fall very heavily on agriculture, which generally speaking should not be taxed at the present time. We cannot altogether escape from taxing people engaged in agriculture, but we do not aim to tax them, if we can help it, until conditions in agriculture are much better than they are now. We deliberately decided that it would be better to increase the national defence tax, a tax which we will take in from week to week and month to month. We do not have to wait for it as we do for income tax until some time next spring, April or May, or perhaps later, depending on whether or not the tax is paid by instalments, and as we would have to wait for an increased sales tax. Rightly or wrongly we have decided that this is a fairer and a better tax because it will tax the persons who are actually in receipt of increased incomes. We think that is better than a
tax that is spread unscientifically, wastefully and uneeonomically over a lot of people irrespective of whether or not they have any net income.
I may be asked: Then why do you not take off the eight per cent sales tax? We cannot do that because our requirements are too great. The time may come when we shall have to increase it. We may have to impose taxation where we can get the money regardless of the effects. But certainly I would not be disposed to favour increasing the sales tax until we had increased the national defence tax.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister's whole argument is based on the necessity for increasing the revenue. We will not dispute that: he has to have so much money. But my argument looked to alleviation for those in the very low income brackets, and a complete answer to my plea would be to raise the exemption. You will get the man higher up all right. You will get the minister and you will get me. But raise the non-taxable amount, which in the case of single persons has now been increased to $660, a little higher. Many of these people are in receipt of income for the first time, and they will have to pay perhaps twenty per cent or more of their total income in taxation, direct and indirect.

I want to give an example to the minister to show how unfair the tax can be in its application. When I was home a commercial traveller came to see me. He draws a salary of something like $2,500 a year. Some two years ago he had the misfortune to lose his wife. He has a family of three, all over twenty-one years of age, therefore he receives no exemption for them. Naturally he wants to keep his family together and he is compelled to keep a housekeeper. He told me that this tax, if raised to seven per cent, would be a severe hardship on him. He finds it difficult enough to pay the tax when it is three per cent. He has a brother who lives not far away from him. The brother has a wife and family, and the question this commercial traveller asked me was this:	"Why
should I, who now .have to keep a stranger in my home to look after my family while I am on the road travelling, have to pay over 100 per cent more taxation than my brother, under this schedule?"
I realize that the minister has quite a problem. There will be those who will try to chisel and to escape paying their just taxation, but on the other hand there are a large number of people like the gentleman to whom I have just referred who have been living in the one home for many years. I do not know just what the minister can do about it. He has to get the money, I know, and I am not
Income War Tax Act

rising to tell him what to do. I can see that his problem is great. On the other hand I can see injustice and unfairness in the way the tax works out in the case of these two brothers, and it is just an example of perhaps thousands of other cases.
Mr. O'NEILL: I quite appreciate that it is difficult for the minister to arrange taxes that will meet with the approval of everybody, but certain well-defined principles were laid down by the Minister of Finance in discussing the national defence tax. In respect of income tax the principle is laid down that a married man shall be exempt up to $1,500. If he makes $1,600 he pays income tax on the extra $100 over $1,500. But when you come to the national defence tax, his exemption is $1,200. That is too low, and I think it was too low last year. I offer as a solution that you tax those who have an income in excess of $3,000 *the amount necessary to make up the $80,000,000-in short, tax the people who are able to pay. A married man with an income of $1,200, that is $100 a month, pays no national defence tax, but a man making $105 a month, or $1,260, a year is taxed five per cent, not on the $60 by which his income exceeds $1,200, but on the whole $1,260, thus reducing his salary to $100 a month.
Here are the principles which were laid down by the Minister of Finance with regard to the national defence tax. I quote his own words:
In fact, I am sure that a sudden inroad upon established arrangements of society would create so much dislocation that it would do more harm than good to our war effort. In imposing taxation of this kind some regard must be had to the manner of life in the country.
It would seem that we have to have regard for the manner of life of the rich people, but we do not have regard for the poor people who are trying to raise families on $100 a month. The government taxes everything they make over $100.
Then, again quoting the minister, and referring particularly to the argument he used to substantiate his position respecting income tax, we find this:
_ If you have a ten per cent rate on a lower income and a sixty per cent rate on a higher income, when you double the ten per cent rate you cannot double the sixty per cent rate.
Quite obviously you cannot do that; but in changing from the income tax to the national defence tax the minister has done just that. It has been increased, not twice, but by a thousand per cent. The minister takes it all; he leaves nothing to the chap making $105 a month. We see abundant evidence that our past system has been very faulty.

We start taxing people at a point in their income when they cannot provide themselves with the necessities of life. I do not believe any reasonable argument can be advanced to show that- the government is doing anything other than that very thing. The number of young men who go up for examination to the army and who are found to be unfit for army service is deplorable. In a great many instances their, condition is due to bad teeth. Those people have never had a chance. On an income of only $100 a month a man with a wife and two children cannot possibly provide the necessities of life and pay for dental and medical attention. It is an impossibility. All those things have to go by the board. But now, when the minister requires $80,000,000-and I agree that we do require $80,000,000-he is putting the tax in the wrong place. He is putting it where it will injure the young men and women of the country by reducing their incomes to the point where they cannot provide the necessities of life.
The national defence tax should not be imposed on married persons with incomes of less than $1,500. Even then it should be imposed only on the amount of income beyond the exempted sum, not on the whole income. It has been said that we must give consideration to the standard of living which has prevailed in Canada. If that consideration must be applied to persons receiving incomes of $40,000, $50,000 or $60,000, why should it not also apply to those who receive only $1,000, $1,200 or $1,500? The same yardstick should be used all the way through. I appeal to the minister to give further consideration to the national defence tax. It is the only point in the budget on which I have any serious disagreement with the minister.
There are some other things I should like to see done, but in this one instance we are not only injuring the people; we are injuring the war effort, we are injuring the nation, we are injuring the whole cause, because we are reducing the standard of living of our people.

Mr. Chairman, I agree with what has been said by the hon. member for Kamloops. Is it intended by this tax to raise money or to reduce purchasing power? I agree that it may have the effect of reducing purchasing power to a point where the morale of the people will suffer. If the purpose of the tax is only that of obtaining $80,000,000, there are other ways of getting that amount of money.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We think it is desirable to prevent the possibility of too abundant purchasing. The condition seems to be that

Income War Tax Act
retail sales have gone up very rapidly, and are still running away above what they were a year ago.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Of beer, increase of from 25 to 33^ per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: And automobiles.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, one could name a
large number of expansions in expenditures on the part of our people. If that were not curbed to some extent by taxation we would rapidly drift into a state of inflation. I believe all hon. members, including the hon. member who has just spoken and the group to which he belongs, agree that that would be extremely serious, and that it should not happen. There are two objectives, the first to get money, and the second to prevent such a heavy demand upon material and labour resources which might in this way be diverted from the war effort. I think all hon. members agree that this is an end to which government policy should be directed. To achieve this end we have to tax heavily.

Is the increase the minister has mentioned an increase in the aggregate, or on a per capita basis? It is understandable that there would be an increase in the aggregate, because of the number of people who are now employed and who were formerly out of work. I am asking, however, if there is also a per capita increase, and to what extent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should think so, yes. It seems to me the conclusion is inescapable.

I feel very much as does the leader of the opposition with respect to this national defence tax. I realize of course that the minister must have money. At the same time we are imposing tax after tax. The minister says we must in every possible way avoid inflation.
I said the other day I hoped we would have an opportunity to discuss some of the regulations put into effect by order in council and under the control of the Minister of Labour. We have not yet had that opportunity. These regulations predicate the whole cost of living upon five different items. The fact is that there are a dozen items not mentioned at all. There is no mention of dental care, medical care, drugs, and many other things one could mention. All these services are a crying necessity for any family or individual.
The minister states that we must avoid inflation. If there is one thing which will cause inflation, surely it is the act of continually reaching into a man's pay envelope 14873-180
and taking something out of it. He must of necessity demand more wages. He must have enough money to live on. He must have enough money to keep his family comfortable. The result is that we will hear demands for higher wages, and the beginning of the spiral of inflation. We know it has already started. More than that, appeals have been made to people working in industry to contribute to war service funds. I do not think there has ever been a finer response by industrial office workers than there was in the last six months.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is the hon. member referring to the purchases of war savings certificates?
I am referring to the donations to the war services. We know of factory after factory where one hundred per cent of the employees contributed to the united war services appeal and to the Red Cross.
And the contributions are deducted weekly.

Besides that, most industries have reached eighty per cent, some of them one hundred per cent, in their purchases of war savings certificates. True, it is a saving; but that much money is being taken out of pay envelopes.
Weekly.

These subscriptions reduce the amount of money left to a man to maintain his family. It makes it more difficult for him to do things for his family which he has not been able to do for many years. It makes it more difficult for him to pay some of his old debts. I know this to be true, from experience in our own industry, where we have employed people who had been .'unemployed for years. As the Minister of Labour has pointed out, unemployment insurance will begin to operate on July 1. Once more we are going to invade the pay envelope of industrial and office workers. I realize that the minister must have money, but if he is not prepared to extend the amount of exemption, levying the tax on all sums above that, why not do as some members in this party suggested in the budget debate? Why not pay back to the employees, in the form of a certificate, which does not have to be interestbearing, a certain percentage of the increase in national defence tax, so that at the end of the war they will receive a part of that money as a saving? Surely we have to do something. You cannot stop inflation. The war-time prices and trade board, according to a statement in this morning's press, say that they cannot control the rising price of meat.

Income War Tax Act

The Department of Labour declares that the cost of living has gone up five or six per cent. That is ridiculous; we know it has gone up much more than that.
Eight per cent.
More than eight per cent.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Ten per cent.

Yes, and it has gone up more than ten per cent. The cost of living has gone away up. Clothing, shoes, meat and all the various things that enter into the family budget have risen in price. People are paying these increased prices. The Department of Labour has said to the industrial workers of the country: Your wages are pegged at a certain figure until such time as we think the cost of living has risen above that figure. But the department's method of figuring the cost of living is ridiculous. It is not practical, and certainly it does not give a clear picture of rising prices throughout the country. The minister ought to reconsider section 4 and do something to remove the tremendous burden that is being placed on the wage earners of Canada. We are asking them to bear too heavy a burden in proportion to what they are receiving, having regard to the cost of maintaining their homes and families.
i Mr. GRAYDON: May I follow up what was said by the hon. member for Kamloops? There is a good deal in what he says, and I have heard working men in various industries make the statement on different occasions that there should be a different arrangement in the levying of the tax, so that when a man reaches, say, $660 or more than that, he should not suddenly find himself with his whole income subject to national defence tax. The principle followed for so many years in connection with income tax is entirely different. The exemption is there, but with the national defence tax many people are confused; they do not know why the principle followed in the income tax was departed from. I know that what the hon. member for Kamloops has said is only too true so far as working people are concerned. The committee should carefully review the whole situation with regard to the application of this tax.
In one of the Toronto newspapers in March of this year there appeared a letter from an accountant of that city. I am not going to put the letter on Hansard, because it is lengthy, but there is one paragraph which I think the minister should carefully consider if it is the sort of representation that can be heeded at the moment. In dealing with the question of the national defence tax, from the point of [Mr. Homuth.l
view of an auditor, the writer makes an interesting statement. I happen to have some knowledge of this man which leads me to believe that he is quite reputable, and he has had so much experience that perhaps his suggestions might be considered. He says:
The returns should not be made monthly, as is required at present, but each employer should be required to furnish an estimate payroll and pay tax thereon in advance, similar to the workmen's compensation board. This method would eliminate at least ten returns and acknowledgments during the course of the year and the government would get all the tax during the first seven months. As wages were paid, the employer would deduct the tax payable and make one final return for the year along with an estimate for the following year.
I must plead a good deal of ignorance about accountancy, but knowing the reputation of the man who wrote this letter I felt that in all fairness I should bring his views to the attention of the committee so that the minister, if he desires to do so, might comment on the suggestion. So far as possible we should simplify these things for employer and employee. This is getting now to be a world full of forms, and if we can simplify procedure so much the better. I should like the minister to consider the point raised.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will give it consideration, but I should not care to comment on it at the moment without studying it and thinking about it. Many suggestions have been made for simplifying the administration of the national defence tax, but in some cases the simplicity could be attained only at the expense of fairness. Whether that is so in regard to the suggestion the hon. gentleman has quoted, I do not know.

With reference to the national defence tax, what was the motive behind the change from the principle governing income tax? Under the income tax a definite exemption is allowed and the tax is paid only above the sum exempted. Under the national defence tax you pay the tax on the whole income once you have gone over the exempted amount.
Mr. ILSLEY": If the deduction is to be made at the source, the employer cannot deduct the proper amount if he does not know the sum by which the total earnings in the year will exceed the weekly earnings multiplied by fifty-two, if it is on a weekly basis. Let the hon. gentleman put himself in the position of the employer; would he know, what to deduct? It would be easy enough to deduct two per cent or five per cent from the total amount of the wage if the wage were beyond a certain amount, and send that in, and then have a big refund at the end of the year.

Income War Tax Act
There would then be a refund in every case. But the refund system is a very difficult one to operate, and at any rate it would not be desirable to have a refund in every case. I cannot think at the moment how it could be done without a refund in every case on the principle that has been suggested. Apart from that, if the amount of the tax is small and if the exemption is a proper one, the amount by which the pay is cut down is limited. It cannot go beyond the exemption.
The hon. member for Kamloops cited a case in which the earnings were just over the amount of the exemption, that of a married man earning 8105 a month. There the tax would be such, if he had no children, as to bring him down from around $1,260 to around $1,200, but as soon as he got over the $1,260 he would be keeping nearly all of it. If he earned $1,300 he would not be brought down to $1,200. Then there is the deduction for children as well, so much a child. It would make a tremendous difference in the yield if we changed this system, and it would mean, I think, the filing of returns in all cases and refunds in all cases.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It would mean that the man in the low bracket would not be paying much tax.

I think the
minister is right when he suggests that any minister preparing a budget must keep in mind the fact that during the war we are increasing the amount of money going into circulation in the form of wages without proportionately increasing the amount of consumers' goods available; consequently unless we can restrict the amount spent on consumers' goods we shall have inflation. There is no doubt about that. A very large proportion, something like forty-four per cent, of the goods we are now producing are not consumers' goods but war goods. The question arises whether the national defence tax is the best way to restrict that consumption.
It seems to me there are two things to keep in mind, and the first is whether or not at the present time we are producing the maximum of consumers' goods of which we are capable, having in mind the fact that certain commodities are necessary for war purposes. It seems to me that we have not yet begun really to tap the productive capacity of the Canadian economy with reference to consumers' goods, because we have, or had this winter, in the neighbourhood of 300,000 people on relief. Assuming one employable person to a family of five, this means there are 50,000 to
60,000	people who could still go into production. Isn't it something we ought to investigate? Before we talk about restricting consumption we should find out whether or not we are really using our productive machinery to its full capacity, having in mind always that you cannot take commodities required for war purposes, such as steel.
The second question is this: what class of people can best afford to endure a restriction of consumption? I agree with the hon. member for Kamloops that the group which will be immediately affected by this national defence tax, those just above the border-line, consists of those who can least afford to have their consumption restricted. Everyone knows that large numbers of them have only come into employment during the last year or two, and there is a tremendous back-log, as has already been mentioned, in the matter of medical and dental care. There are also house furnishings, clothing, dishes, a score of things left practically untouched through the depression. To restrict the consuming power of this group i3 a very serious matter.
The minister is right in saying that it is not enough merely to object; some alternative must be offered. I am not suggesting that this can be a complete answer, but the other day the minister placed on Hansard at page 2771, a table showing the distribution of wealth in Canada. From that it appears that the maldistribution of wealth is even worse than most of us imagined. The table shows that 42-3 per cent of the people of Canada get only 16-73 per cent of the wealth that comes within this category. Or if you add the first two lines together you find that 65-7 per cent of the people receive 33-6 per cent of the wealth. Is it not a fact that, before any employee who believes he has overpaid his national defence tax can make a claim for rebate, he must fill out a form which the department provides, which also is an income tax return, because he cannot ask for a refund on his national defence tax until he has shown the department what income he earned? From what I know of our local district, I fear that the department will be inundated with the number of applications for refund of tax, ranging all the way from a few cents up to several dollars.
I feel that employers should be given some leeway in this matter. At present they are allowed none. If to-day an employee earns during two or three weeks an amount which, if earned throughout the year, would make him subject to tax, that tax must be paid; under the act the employer has no alternative. The employer has been made more or less responsible for the collection of that tax; and if he were given some leeway in the matter he would be in a position to say, "Well, now, I doubt if this man or this woman is going to be subject to the tax. I will let it go until toward the end of November; I will not take it off merely for the two or three weeks in which they may have earned that amount". Then, in November, if the employee's earnings are sufficient to subject him to the tax, the amount could be deducted from his pay from then until the end of the year. Such an arrangement would save the department a tremendous amount of work. Under the act as it stands the employer has no leeway at all; it says that he must deduct the tax from the wage of the employee.

The difficulty I find with ny hon. friend's suggestion is this. Suppose the employee worked three weeks at one place, then departed to another city, remained idle for two weeks, got a steady job for six months, and then changed his job again, the department would have no control at all as regards the tax due from him.
Mr. O'BRIEN: I suggest that the workman might be given some sort of small book; a standardized form in the nature of a savings bank-book might be prepared and sold for not more than five or ten cents, which the employee could retain, because, as an employee travels from Halifax to Vancouver, working in the course of a year for eight or ten or a dozen employers, it is going to be a fantastic task for the department to check any statements he makes, and some of the statements might be based on pure fiction.

There are a great many people employed on small wages who do not understand the principle of this refund. I have spoken to some of them in the last week. In British Columbia we -have a tax known as the one per cent wage tax. I see the hon. member for Yale looking at me and perhaps wondering what I am going to say in that connection. Later, that tax was modified in this way: The one per cent tax on wages is still collected, but at the end of the year everybody in British Columbia is supposed to show in their income tax returns whether they made sufficient money to pay income tax. Then the finance department of the province, if they find that sufficient wages were not earned to pay income tax, refund what -has been paid in the one per cent wage tax. If the employee has made sufficient in wages to pay income tax, then what he has paid in the one per -cent wage tax is credited to his income tax payments, and if he has paid more in the wage tax than he is called upon to pay in income tax, the province refunds the difference to him. The national defence tax could be handled in exactly the same way. It has not been found impossible or too expensive to handle the wage tax in British Columbia in that way, or it would have been done away with. They still retain that system and refund whatever amount is shown to have been overpaid.
Reference has been made to inflation; but if .you permit these people, many of whom have been out of work for long periods of time, to spend money that they are now earning, you are not going to have inflation. That is not true of the majority of the people in my riding by any means, nevertheless I know that there are in my constituency many homes where as soon as the weather gets cold the children cannot go to school because they have no boots. I am not saying that in order to lead people to believe that that applies geenerally ',o the people of my constituency because it

certainly does not. There are, however, a great many homes where the children have only one suit of clothes, and the washing has to be done at night so that the clothing will be ready to put on again in the morning. When the earning power of these people is increased, naturally the first thing they do is to buy an extra suit of clothes, or a pair of boots for the children, or something for the wife or husband. That is going to increase sales in this country.
If the minister feels that he must keep down incomes in order to avoid inflation, I suggest that the money which the department takes away from these people by way of national defence tax on income over $1,200 be invested in war savings certificates and that, when the war is over, it * be paid back to these people. There will be no inflation if that is done, and it would hold out some hope to these people. What hope have they now, after having been out of a job for six or ten years? I know men working on the two transcontinental roads who, with the exception of two or three weeks' work in rush seasons, have not had a job in ten years. Now they get a job. Naturally they are going to start to build up their run-down household, which is the proper thing for them to do, and when the government starts in and takes this tax away from them just when they have at last got a job, it discourages them and they can see no daylight' at all. I strongly suggest that the Minister of Finance, if he wishes to prevent inflation, should say to these people who are paying national defence tax: "We are not letting you spend this money, but we are going to set it aside, and every time you pay in $5 in national defence tax, we shall set it aside for you in war savings certificates which will be given back to you when the war is over." I am sure that would be a gesture which would be well received by the people of this country.

Now that we are pondering the problems of those in the lower income brackets, it seems to me that we should attempt to unscramble 'our own positions as members of parliament. We, of course, have to pay the national defence tax, and I wish it to be clearly understood that I am not objecting to paying that tax, but I am objecting to the method by which the tax is collected. I seriously doubt whether it is constitutional. When the form was given to me last July I called on several officials until I finally got in touch with a well known and most efficient official in the national revenue department, and I asked him by whom I was employed. His reply was that I was employed by the crown. If we as members of parliament elected in a democracy are considered, even technically, as being employed by the crown and the indemnity we receive is in any way construed to be a salary, this parliament is perhaps sitting unconstitutionally. That may be a highly technical point, but, after all, in the days of Cromwell this very question became a national issue. We should be consistent in this house. The so-called indemnity which we receive is really only to indemnify the member for the loss of his time in coming here to serve his majesty in the running of the country, and if that indemnity is construed as salary, the very basis of the democracy for which we are fighting to-day goes down to the graveyard.

We may have to follow German methods yet. We have to match wits with them. Sometimes it is necessary to use poison as an antidote to poison. Whether you accept their methods or not, they are not concerned with our methods. We have to get the money to win this war. I believe it would be to the advantage of the committee to have the information appearing in this article. I am prepared to admit that it was published on June 30, 1939, and there is no doubt there have been vast increases in taxation, even in Germany, since that time. Some hon. members opposite have taken exception to the distribution of wealth. In the practical application of any kind of tax there is always that something which cannot be put down in an account book. For instance, in the occupational groups I find the largest group paying income tax in 1939 and 1940 was that known as the middle-class, and they are classified as employees. They numbered 227,261, and comprised seventy-seven per cent of the total number of individuals paying income taxes. We would not expect many millionaires in that class. I know it is considered good sport nowadays to take a potshot at a millionaire. It seems to be a rather popular amusement. I do not happen to be in that class, and I believe I can view it from a sufficient distance to get a proper focus. They are a valuable group in any country's economy.

It is most useful to have available some men with money, because, after all, this large group of employees have a product, namely labour, which they have to sell to somebody. By virtue of frugality and thrift some men have accumulated wealth sufficient to invest in industry, and they provide a market at which people may sell their labour. One of the smallest groups in the table was that of the agrarians. I believe that an agrarian is a farmer. That group numbered 1.721, or a little over one-half of one per cent of all the individuals paying income tax. But let me qualify that. After all, as I said a few days ago, the farmer has something better than money can buy. With that in mind I would draw the attention of hon. members to the record of property ownership in Ontario as disclosed by the census of 1931. We find that most millionaires are situated in communities with populations exceeding 30,000, and that in those wealthy centres only forty-five per cent of the people own their own homes, while seventy-five per cent of the farmers own their own homes.
