it may be $700,000,000 or $800,000,000 -we shall have to make extensive loans. We shall have to borrow a great deal from the public, something over a billion during the current year.

The minister has-not given a fair picture. If we were to balance our budget and that extra amount over $1,300,000,000 were raised in Canada and used for civilian purposes, the rest that we would raise would not be seventy-eight per cent of the war effort. We are not actually paying seventy-eight per cent of our war effort by taxation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If we were not giving assistance at all to Great Britain, not raising money for that purpose, we would be paying seventy-nine per cent of our war and peace efforts out of taxation at the rate that we are taxing, on the basis of $1,300,000,000.

Almost incredible!

Income War Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: It is easy to ask questions, but sometimes it takes a long while to answer some of them. The question which the hon. gentleman asked me a moment ago is one of those, because there is at stake the principle of paying for this particular war, and we have to do many things which in the ordinary course of events we would not do. Public policy, in many respects, is not very different from the running of one's own business. When the flow of money is greater in consequence of additional expenditure, that is the time when the government should collect some of it, so that when the post-war period comes we shall not find ourselves staggering under an immense debt. If we do not use that money for purposes of taxation we use it in the purchase of goods. That will result in an increased cost of goods to the consumer, absorbing his purchasing power, thus adding to the burden of the government in supplying munitions of war. It is a double-edged sword, and whether the policy is one that I like or not, I do not think there is anything about it that violates any definite principle. With that explanation, I believe the minister is justified in taking the stand he does. I am prepared to support this government on any policy that will enable us to pay as we go. It may be unpopular at the present time; and whether we survive as a party, when the conflict is over, we shall have done something of which we may well be proud. We shall have relieved those who are to follow us of a great deal of the burden that will have to be borne in the post-war period.
Is it not our duty to make it as equitable as possible?

Yes, and I believe that is being accomplished. If you take away all the money from those 483 in the higher brackets, you will kill the goose that lays the golden egg, but it will not go very far in our war expenditure.
Nobody is advocating that.
In the first three categories of that table are to be found what one might term the commonplace people-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: People of low incomes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I say, much more than one-third now.

Yes. I have given these figures roughly, but I think they answer the question of the hon. member and show that the government of the day is going as far as possible towards a fair and equal distribution of the burden.

The minister made an observation a moment ago and gave a percentage. When he gave that percentage he did not carry in his mind the addition to the capital sum of the deficit we shall probably have during the current year. Be that as it may, we have to spend every effort and every dollar necessary to win this conflict, no matter where the money comes from.
I have disposed of the question that had to do with the minister's mathematics. Coming now to the matter of this taxation, my suggestion to the minister would be, "all that the traffic can bear." When I say that I would ask the minister to think it all the way through. A large portion of this tax will come directly or indirectly from industry. From the employees it will, of course, come directly, but indirectly it will come from industry itself. We were all enthusiastic for the war savings certificates, because we thought our employees were making an investment and would get the money back. Industry raised wages and paid the major portion of that. Many of those who did not subscribe found that instead of getting two cents an hour more money in the case of a single man or three cents more in the case of a married man, they got perhaps only one cent, for the reason that the employer thought they were well able to subscribe and did not do so, and therefore their raise in pay did not go to the same extent as in the case of those who subscribed to war savings certificates their twenty-five cents or fifty cents a week.
Income War Tax Act

To come to the defence tax particularly, immediately the budget was announced it was necessary to raise wages again, one cent, two cents, three cents, four cents, five cents an hour. What is the net result of that? No complaint at all; we must have the money to carry on our war effort. Industry does not mind rearranging itself to keep its employees happy and contented. Employers want their employees to feel that they are part and parcel of this war effort and are doing something themselves. And the deduction is made.
But it is more far-reaching than that. This increase in wages, along with general increases in the costs of running any industry, brings the costs a little higher all through the piece, with the result that industry must get a little more for its finished goods. In getting more for its finished goods, it finds that its inventories rise, its accounts receivable rise. Some hon. members will think profits rise, but they do not in the same proportion. The result is that industry finds itself short of liquid capital or liquid surplus on which to borrow from the banks sufficient money to conduct the business. Where do they get the extra money with which to keep their liquid position in a proper ratio? Perhaps from credit balances or profits. But immediately they get it from that source, forty per cent goes to the government-and quite rightly so; I am not objecting. Then they still find themselves in not as sound a liquid position as formerly.
Then in the case of the individual who owns the business, if he is a working partner, or the stockholder who draws out his dividends, he will pay another forty or fifty per cent on the same credit balance. The net result is that business and industry in Canada find themselves unable to expand as they would like, find their borrowing power reduced and often find it very difficult to expand and take on more business. Therefore I say to the minister, "all the traffic will bear", yes; but let him see that he does not, as one hon. gentleman said, kill the goose that lays the golden egg. Do not cripple business so that it has not enough working capital to carry on.
Compared with this, to my mind the war savings plan is much better. Whether or not we should have gone thus far with the defence tax is a question that I have not yet settled in my mind. I suggest that before any further move is made in this direction, consideration be given to the thought that the hon. member for Waterloo South so well expressed, namely, that in taking this tax from the earnings that are exigible, consideration be given to wage-earners with regard to borrowing from them for the duration of the war, so that, when the war is over, they will have some little nest-egg to fall back upon.

Another point I should like to mention is that to my mind an employee's pay envelope is something that should not be touched or tampered with by anyone, not even governments. What do we find in the small towns in which there is perhaps just one industry? Probably that industry owns many of the houses in that town. We find that by agreement the industry arranges to take the rental for the little home off the pay envelope. Very often the industry will have the employees insured for perhaps $1,000; the firm will probably pay twenty-five cents a week of the cost of that, and fifteen cents will be deducted from the employee's pay. That is deduction number two. Then the employer will probably bring in a car of hard coal and distribute it among his employees, and there will be a wage deduction for the coal. Then they have probably arranged to have a deduction made for war savings certificates. There is a deduction for the national defence tax.
And war services.

On July 1
next there will be a deduction for unemployment insurance. Moreover, in all these communities we have campaigns for community welfare and the Red Cross, and these services advocate that arrangements be made by employers to ask their employees to permit a small deduction each week from their pay for these services. The net result is that the amount actually received may be only half the man's actual pay. Most of these deductions are quite all right, but I say it is wrong to interfere in any way with a man's pay envelope, which I would almost say ought to be regarded as something sacred; and the housewife should not be asked to become a chartered accountant in order to ascertain whether or not her husband was bringing home all his pay every Saturday.
The hon. member for Brant told us that we were almost balancing our budget at the present time.
No; I did not use that term.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
The reasons
just given by the minister were exactly my reasons for objecting to the hon. member for Brant quoting the figures he did, because it seemed to me that Canada's war effort must include all the commitments which are made, particularly the money we must raise to meet Great Britain's account, and it would be most mischievous to have the impression go across the country that we were raising by means of taxation, seventy per cent of all the money we need. If we made that statement, it would become most difficult to raise the loan that will be launched next June or July, and that was why I objected to the statement made by the hon. member. All of Canada's war effort must be included, and that means a great deal more than was covered by our budget or by the war appropriation bill.
Having in mind the thesis on which the minister is basing this taxation, that of restricting the consumption of consumer goods; and having in mind the plea made by the hon. member for Kamloops with regard to setting money aside by means of war savings certificates, I presume the government has given consideration to what is generally called the
Keynes plan of deferred payment. I wonder whether the minister would be prepared to say whether that plan has been considered, what are the objections to adopting it, and whether the government has considered the possibility of adopting it at some time in the near future.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know that I can make any statement on that point. We are not adopting that plan; we are not agreeing to pay back later any part of the amounts being raised by taxation. If we did that at any time I am afraid it would be necessary to increase considerably the amount we are taking from the people. It is not just as easy as hon. gentlemen seem to think. These amounts are being raised on taxation principles, not on loan principles; they are amounts which, generally speaking, the public can pay. This is a load the public can bear; it is not the sort of load that will crush people. We believe they can stand it because of the increased national income; and a great many people will have a good deal of money left. To them we are going and asking for loans. We are still on the voluntary system, not the compulsory system, with regard to loans.
In England they have instituted the compulsory system in a very minor degree. Perhaps this is not exactly the resolution under which this question should be discussed, but I should like to point out that in Great Britain their recent compulsory loans from companies have amounted to nothing but this: they are agreeing to pay back to the companies twenty per cent of the one hundred per cent excess profits tax. In England they have a one hundred per cent excess profits tax, and they have decided that this is too much to take and keep. The chancellor of the exchequer made that very clear in his speech, which I have before me; and because of the fact that in a great many instances companies would not be able to establish the necessary reserves and so on, in his budget the chancellor of the exchequer provided that, after the war, twenty per cent of that one hundred per cent excess profits tax would be repaid to the companies.
In this country we have a different system. Our total excess profits tax is 79-5 per cent. There is still 19-5 per cent left which we will ask companies to lend us voluntarily to the extent that they are able to do so. We will get a great deal of that; and we will get a great deal more from individuals. The two systems are not so very much different in amount in that regard. They are different in principle, the principle in this country being
Income War Tax Act

that here we are taxing, which means that we are taking the money we think the people can pay in taxation, without assuming an obligation to repay that money, and we are asking the people to lend us further amounts. If they respond perfectly, each in accordance with his ability, it will be a much better adjusted scheme than a system under which compulsion is adopted, because when compulsion is adopted there is the probability of a great many harsh cases arising. For instance, take the case of a man who has sickness, with perhaps two or three members of his family ill; or the case of a man who has heavy debts. It would be very difficult to make allowance for such cases because one cannot make general rules which will cover them. Then if you take away from that man by forced loan as much as you take from his neighbour, who has no sickness and no debts, you are apt to crush him.

In connection with
the matter raised by the hon. member for Yorkton, I find that a great many farmers still are unaware of the existence of this tax. Has the minister any information to give us indicating the percentage of farmers across Canada who have made returns in accordance with the requirements of this act? I notice that section 5 requires that every employer shall deduct at the source if the rate of pay of the employee is such as, if continued for three months, would cause the annual earnings of the employee to be in excess of the amount mentioned in subsection 1 thereof. I observe that there are notices in post offices across the country, but at meetings which I have held I found that very few farmers know that they are supposed to deduct from employees the national defence tax. When we were discussing this last year I understood that, if a man engaged an employee for even one day and paid him the rate set forth in the act, be would be required to make the deduction, and later the employee could apply for repayment. I understand that later some changes were made in the regulations. Would the minister state, first, what has been the response from the farmers aero* the country, and, second, how many days does an employer have to employ a man before he is expected to make the return?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
One day, if he pays him at the rate of $600 a year. There is no information as to the number of farmers who have filed returns. The commissioner tells me that he has not any information on that. It may be possible, by going through the returns and looking at the occupations of the persons making them, to compile that information, but I should think it would be quite a job,

and it would not give any indication as to the proportion of those, liable to make returns, who have made returns.

I wonder what efforts have been put forward, apart from the notices in the press and in the post offices, to make known the existence of this tax.
Mr..MAYHEW: What value should we put upon the board and lodging provided by the farmer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There was a brochure, widely circulated, which dealt with all these matters. I remember that it was discussed last year in this chamber. I cannot give the hon. member the figures. There was a question asked last year by the hon. member for Battle River with regard to the board and lodging of hired men. I think it is dealt with in a publication of the Department of National Revenue, income tax division. We discussed it fully here last year, and then this publication was issued and circulated. I do not believe that there has been any newspaper advertising bringing this matter specifically to the attention of employers, farmers or otherwise.
The amount was $20 to $25, was it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have forgotten.
Is the rate for urban and rural employers the same?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Department of Labour was consulted, and a classification was made and some latitude given. There is a difference provided for between different localities, various parts of the country. I cannot give the hon. gentleman accurate information, but I know it is available.

Before the resolution
passes, would the minister give at least a reasonably close estimate of what the difference would be to the treasury if the exemption w7ere raised from $660 to $750? Undoubtedly $660 is a very low figure, and we must have specific information showing what is involved before we can intelligently consider whether the exemption should be raised to $750.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister said that he would not raise it.
Then he himself must have figures. His decision cannot be based on mere guesswork.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think we can make some kind of estimate. I shall try to get it if the hon. member wants it. It would not be very accurate.

Undoubtedly there is a feeling in this chamber that $660 is not much of an income for a person to maintain himself

Income War Tax Act
*or herself upon, especially when, as is the case with many girls in offices, and young men, the employee has to contribute in support of the home something more than would ordinarily be involved for board and lodging. If it does not make a great deal of difference to the revenue, I think we should consider establishing a higher minimum bracket, and if necessary, put the national defence tax at a higher rate. It may be the purpose of the minister to employ this arrangement as an anti-inflation measure rather than as a revenue-raising device. As I have said, however, we cannot as business men give this question intelligent consideration unless we know what amount is involved.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall try to give some sort of estimate.

In listening to this discussion I am rather confused, and in my own case a question arises which I should like to have cleared up. I happen this year to be hiring men by the day and by the month. I am also getting work done by men under a contract. For instance, take seeding; I contracted to have so much land seeded for a given amount, over SI,200. I have already made an advance to the man who has undertaken the work; the job is finished, and in the next few days I shall have to make the final payment. I am also hiring men by the day, paying them $2.50 and $3, to do certain work, and they will work for me for probably two or three weeks. Do I take it that I have to make the deduction from the man who is working for me by the day, when I pay him, because if he worked for a full year he would receive over $600?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is he a single man?
No; he is a married man.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

I have others working for me who are single men. How do I stand with respect to the man who is doing my seeding? While I am citing my own case, probably there are other farmers here who are in the same position. This man contracted to do a certain job for a certain amount. Have I to deduct this tax from my payment to him?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is the person who is doing the work for you your employee?
Well, I have an agreement with him to do certain work, to do a certain operation within a given time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If the man is not the employee of the hon. member, the hon. member does not have to make the deduction; but if the man is an employee, the hon.
member does, even though the man is engaged for only a week or two, if the rate of pay would amount to $600 a yen'-.
In that case he would be termed a contractor?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, I will say it again. It is only in the case of an employee. In case the hon. gentleman wants to look it up, it is section 91 of the Income War Tax Act, under part XV, dealing with the national defence tax, subsection 5:
Every employer at the time of payment of earnings to an employee shall deduct and collect the tax imposed on the employee under this section in respect of earnings of the employee earned and accruing due during and after July, 1940, for each period covered by the payments, if the rate of pay of the employee is such that if continued for twelve months would cause the annual earnings of the employee to be in excess of the relevant amount mentioned in subsection one hereof.
If, instead of employing the person as an employee, he makes a contract with someone who is an independent contractor, that person is not his employee, and the amount he pays that contractor is not deductible.
I have an agreement in writing.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The test is. I think, is it master and servant relationship?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In that case, that would be so.
If the information for which I have asked is not forthcoming, might I point out that it is six o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I want to make an announcement on another matter. The taxation on soldiers' fares has been receiving consideration, and I was in hopes we would have reached the resolution soon. Apparently, however, it will not be reached until next week, and therefore I want to announce now that I intend, when the resolutions under the Special War Revenue Act come up for consideration, to move an amendment that the tax imposed on transportation tickets will not apply to members of his majesty's armed forces in uniform, when proceeding on leave. I take it from the speeches urging this step which have been made by members from all quarters of the house that I am perfectly safe in seeing to it that this change goes into effect just as soon as the transportation companies can be notified. It will be an extraordinary step to take, but I feel perfectly justified in taking it in view of the expression of opinion from all sides of the house.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall the resolution
carry?

Before the resolution carries, I should like to ask two or three questions. It was not made entirely clear, at least to my satisfaction, whether we are imposing such taxes as this one in resolution 5 mainly to raise money or mainly to curtail purchasing power. I assume the minister would answer that we are imposing the tax for both purposes. Is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Correct, yes.
First of all, to raise money, and next, to curtail purchasing power?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Our object in reducing purchasing power is to prevent inflation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
That is the second point.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To prevent inflation and to make available for the prosecution of the war effort our resources in labour and material to the extent that they are required.

That is consistent with what the minister has said since the beginning. If that is the situation, then all of us agree, I suppose, that inflation is a rise in price which results mainly from a scarcity of goods. We would be safe in assuming, would we not, that that is the meaning of inflation?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No.
Well, unless we take that as a definition, it is difficult to be consistent, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

If we are curtailing purchasing power to prevent people from buying goods, and thereby preventing a shortage of goods from developing, with a rise in price, we must assume that inflation is, in effect, a rise in price resulting from scarcity of goods. That is consistent, is it not? I must say that I have a little difficulty in following the minister's reasoning, and it seems to me important, in the interests of the country and of all hon. members, to be clear about this, so that all of us will be thinking along the same lines.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We have gone over it very often. If you put into circulation a lot of money; if everyone has plenty of money and starts to buy goods, the price of goods is very

likely to go up. There may not be, in one sense, any scarcity of goods, although perhaps there are not all the goods that everybody would like to have at that moment. If hon. gentlemen wish to call that condition a scarcity, perhaps it is. Certainly we do not think it would be a good thing to have great numbers of people working to produce goods to meet that civilian need, when they ought to be producing goods to meet the war-time need.

That is quite in accord with what the minister has said. I believe that right here there lies a principle upon which we can build a sort of solution for our difficulties. I may be wrong, but I am strongly of that opinion. I am glad to see that the leader of the opposition is in his seat, so that we can all talk this over together.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Leave me out of this!

No matter how much money there is in circulation, if there are more goods in the country of any particular kind than people wish to buy, the price of those particular goods will not rise. For example, I assume that, with the quantity of potatoes we have in Canada, the price would not rise even though we had twice the amount of money in circulation that we have at present. The reason is that we have so many potatoes that people can buy all they 'want, and still there would be more than they can consume. The same thing would be true of wheat and wheat products. It seems to me important that we should clearly understand this point. I must say that, listening to most of the hon. members who speak in this chamber, I gather that there is a general inability to face this fact. If what I have said is true, that the price will not rise unless there is a relative scarcity of goods, then, before we assume that we need to reduce the purchasing power of the people we should look to our supply of goods. If we find that that supply is sufficient to meet the needs of the people, there is no need to reduce the purchasing power of the people because of those goods.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to get into a Socratic discussion here of abstract principles; but there are not enough goods in the country. We must import from abroad very, very large quantities.

There is no desire,
Mr. Chairman, to get into any discussion of abstract principles. I believe, however, that there is a failure on the part of most of our economists, most of our thinkers, to comprehend the real cause of the rise in price, the real cause of inflation. In Canada to-day

Income War Tax Act
inflation is setting in for two reasons. There may be scarcity in the case of some commodities; but in respect of some other commodities the cost of production is being increased by taxation to the extent that there is a rise in price because of that. If the government fails to recognize these two facts, it can make some grave mistakes in levying these taxes, and I would say right at this point that this particular tax is one in respect of which the government, unless it realizes the truth of what I have said, can make as grave a mistake as has been made in this country in the last fifty years.
Suppose you take potatoes, butter, eggs, milk, cheese, cream, all kinds of garden vegetables, and a great many kinds of fruit, as well as a wide variety of other commodities;
I say that there is not in the hands of the people enough money to buy the supply of these goods which we have on hand. If we reduce the amount of purchasing power in the hands of the people which could be used in the purchase of these goods, we are making a serious mistake.
I am not trying to advocate any particular theory. Of course, the recognition of the fact I am endeavouring to demonstrate lies at the basis of my own theory; but we do. not need to be advocating social credit in order to talk good, sound sense and good management, economically speaking, in this country. There are principles which apply independently of any particular theory. Not long ago I was talking to a man who had invested a certain amount of money in a plant in order to increase bis production, on the assumption that thereby, if he could sell his goods, he could reduce his overhead and his costs of production; but the taxes which the government is imposing are limiting the amount of goods which he can sell. The result is that instead of being able to cut down overhead and make a profit because of that additional investment, he actually has his overhead increased and loses because of the investment, and his concern is likely to be wrecked. This is very important.
I would say that to impose a tax on so low an income as $660 a year, if it is imposed from the point of view of limiting consumption, is a serious mistake. If it is imposed in order to raise revenue, that is another matter. I wonder whether I make myself clear. I agree that there are certain commodities which we are importing from abroad and there are commodities of which we have not enough, and probably to manufacture which we would have to use material and man-power which we cannot afford to use. As regards these commodities it is necessary to limit consumption. But this method of limiting it is, in
my opinion, wrong. If we want to limit the purchase of automobiles let us put on a quota, let us ration automobiles. If we want to limit the purchase of stoves or of refrigerators, let us ration these commodities. But do not let us, in seeking to restrict stoves, impose such a tax as will prevent people from buying strawberries, apples, butter and wheat. That is the very thing that will happen as a result of the tax.

In what I have to say on
this point I desire to make two things clear. In the first place, I do not reach my conclusion along the economic philosophy of the leader of the Social Credit party who has just spoken, nor do I subscribe to the economic doctrines of his group. The second point I wish to make clear is that I subscribe to the budget and its principles, and I believe our Minister of Finance has made a wonderful contribution, in the very difficult problem which he has set out to solve.
There are two respects in which I differ from his principle in some minor details which I will discuss later on, but I wish to go on record in this regard. I do not subscribe at all to the economic theory that a man whose net income is $660 a year, having a family if you like, a wife and two children-
No; single men.

Well, then, take the lower brackets where you reach the man with a family, whose income is $1,200. That we should attempt to discipline either of these men by telling them that it is bad for them to have a little more money than that to spend is something with which I do not agree. I thought we had been endeavouring in this country for many years to increase the spending capacity of eighty per cent of the people, who are borrowers, who are in debt, people who have to struggle and battle for existence. Instead of now attempting to act as schoolmaster to them and to tell them that it will be bad for them to have a little more money to spend, we should direct our taxation, for the raising of funds to carry on our war effort, to those-and this has already been embodied in the policy-who are best able to pay. I believe we are adopting a false economy when we attempt to indicate to the people that one of the great purposes of this taxation is to restrict the capacity to buy goods for the home and for the ordinary needs of the man who has a sparse income and is in debt.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We are not attempting to say to any man that it is bad for him to buy goods, and I certainly do not want my position to be represented to the public as being
Income War Tax Act

anything like that. I did say that there were two purposes in these taxes, and there are two purposes. Whether the purpose of the tax in the low category is to curtail consumption or not, I am not prepared to say. It is hard to 'be absolutely definite about purposes. The main immediate purpose is to raise a tremendous sum of money and to go down to the point where there is a large number of people who are earning the money. The hon. gentleman started to say that a married man with children, supporting them on $660, would be taxed. That is a mistake. The limit there is $1,200; we are not bringing everyone down to $660. Moreover, there is $20 credit for each child. Opinions will differ as to where the line should be drawn, but it is drawn at a higher level this year than it was last year, at $600. I do not know how we are going to make out if we do not do some taxing of these lower incomes. Of course, I have no doubt that members of the house, if we were to put the matter to a vote, would say that we should make it $700 or $750 or $800, but there is a grave responsibility in getting money.

I wish to direct attention to a grave evil and injustice under the regulations as they stand. I refer to the deductions at present made on the wages of people, many hundreds of thousands of which never reach $600 for single men, or $1,200 in the case of married men. Under the present regulations, each employer deducts the amount of two per cent defence tax, and the labourer is under a serious handicap because he does not understand the regulations, and in the majority of cases does not realize that he is entitled to a refund if at the end of the year his income does not reach $600, or $1,200 if he is a married man. Would the minister consider making a statement at the present time to clarify this regulation with regard to that refund? What are the dates within which the worker must make his set annual income? I believe this tax went into force in July, 1940. Second, will the minister make a statement as to the procedure that must be followed for the worker to procure the refund? Third, what about the onus of proof? Must the worker present vouchers to show that the two per cent has been deducted? I believe that is the situation with those who have to pay income tax. If every employer in Canada has to send in returns with regard to every person he employs, and every worker must make application to the federal department for his refund, we must have a terrific bureaucracy. From the returns given in Hansard at page 2992, I believe there must be $200,000,000 paid out in wages to labourers each year. Five per

cent of that would be $10,000,000, which the worker has paid in, on the assumption that he comes under the tax, although he is supposed to make application for refund. I am quite sure that many employers in Canada are not sending in returns.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Why does the hon. member say that?

Because I know that many farmers in the west who employ men in threshing do not know about the regulation and do not know they are supposed to take that off. I am sure that there are hundreds and thousands of men across this country, the large bulk of casual workers, who do not know that they are to get this money back if their annual income is below $600 or $1,200.
That is where ignorance is bliss.

I do not think it is bliss for these men to be done out of $10,000,000. Would the minister be prepared to make a statement as to what can be done to clarify this matter, so that the workers may know? I think the whole scheme is an extremely poor one because it deals largely with taxing men ' who are not in reality taxable under any defence tax since their wages do not reach the minimum.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know just what statement I can make in addition to those I have made. I stated this afternoon that the Department of National Revenue has issued a publication which explains this whole matter, and which has, I assume, received wide distribution. I can tell the committee in addition to what I have already said that refunds cannot be made until the returns are received from employers giving lists of the employees to whom they have paid wages from which they have made deductions. Those returns are still coming in.
They must be in for the end of the year by now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know. They come in about the end of March.
Do not employers have to make returns every month? In that event the return for January must have come in two months ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, they do, but in order to make the refund the department must have returns from numerous employers.

I asked the same question this afternoon, and the minister told me there could be no refunds because the year is not up.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I corrected that statement
later. I found that the year ended December 31, not July 1.

The employers made a statement to the income tax division at the end of April of this year, giving a list of men in their employ from whom deductions had been made. The very next resolution, No. 5, sets out that the sum shall be $660 for the calendar year 1941.

This is the first opportunity I have had to say anything on these resolutions, because I was on committee work. I wish to associate myself with what was said by the hon. member for Lethbridge in connection with resolution 5.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I would point out to hon. members that we are on resolution 4. I have tried to have it disposed of, but so far, resolution 4 is still under consideration. I may remind hon. members that we are in committee on the various items of these resolutions. A great deal of discussion of a principle of general application, not directly related to the various resolutions now being studied, has been allowed, which is contrary to standing order 58, subsection 2, which reads:
Speeches in committee of the whole house must be strictly relevant to the item or clause under consideration.
The rule uses the word "strictly." There is a reason for that rule. If we do not adhere to it there is tedious repetition in committee on each item of the general discussions that took place when the budget speech was made and the budget resolutions brought down. Although a certain latitude is given, unless the committee by unanimous consent suspends standing order 58 it is the duty of the Chair to bring that to the attention of hon. members.
We are now studying resolution 4 which purports to raise from two to five per cent, or from three to seven per cent as the case may be, the rate of national defence tax. It is to this that the committee should direct its attention.

Other hon. members may have been tedious in this discussion, but I have not, because I have not had the opportunity. I understood from the discussion since I came in that we were discussing resolution 5. Indeed, I think resolutions 4 and 5 should be discussed together, otherwise they are not understandable.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. member wishes to move that, he may do so, but it must be moved and agreed to by the committee, otherwise I must limit the discussion under the rules.
If you will accept a motion that we discuss resolutions 4 and 5 simultaneously I shall be glad to move that.
Agreed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Maclnnis moves:
That resolutions 4 and 5 be studied together.
Is it the pleasure of the committee to adopt the motion?

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to.
5. That the amount of $600 mentioned in the national defence tax section be raised to $660 for the calendar year 1941 and for each year thereafter.

Resolution 4 raises the national defence tax from two per cent to live per cent, and on single persons receiving incomes of $1,200, from three per cent to seven per cent. Resolution 5 raises the minimum income at which the national defence tax begins from $600 to S660. Last year I took the position that $600 was too low an income to begin at, and I am still convinced that $660 is too low, because $660 in 1941 is no better than or possibly not as good as $600 was in 1940. The rate is now raised. I do not say that the cost of living has risen that much; It may have, when one takes into consideration the particular items that people in this income group use mostly. Then, again, there are several deductions. The great majority of employees-and these people would all be employees-are compelled, whether they want to or not, to buy war savings certificates. There are other items. At the time this tax will go into effect there will be another deduction from their pay, the unemployment insurance tax. That is all right for people who have incomes which enable them to pay a few cents or a few dollars without being hurt. But I would point out that a person receiving an income of $660 must consider every five cent piece he spends.
He must consider every cent.

When he goes into a
restaurant he does not look at the bill of fare for what he likes, he looks for what is cheap. If there is something for thirty cents, something for twenty-five cents and something for twenty cents, while he may like the thirty cent or twenty-five cent choice much better, he will take the twenty cent article.
I am convinced, as I believe I said before, that the minister made an excellent job of drawing up this budget. It must have been a difficult undertaking, and I think he carried it out very well indeed. But it is not a perfect budget, and I am trying to help him to improve it. There are a great many reasons
Income War Tax Act

why we should not further take away from those who have not. I do not know whether the minister understands it, but there is strong class feeling in this country. Perhaps that feeling is no stronger than in other countries, but when people are compelled to live on $500, $400 and even $300 a year, while they see other men with incomes amounting to several hundred thousand dollars a year, we are not going to get the voluntary cooperation of those people. Every cent taken from them is just that much more irritation. In Hansard of Tuesday last, I think it was, I read the defence offered by the minister for not taxing those in the higher income brackets to a greater extent. He pointed out that by greater diligence, greater effort and greater ability these men were able to command a greater income; that they had acquired a certain standard of living, and that it would not do to take away too much from them. I think we are now approximately in the position of being under siege; and when we are besieged, some people are not going to have cake while the rest have crusts. If we have reached the point where we cannot all have cake but we can all have bread, then let us all have bread. The minister said he would not know how to spend an income of $50,000. I wonder whether he would know how to spend an income of $600 or $700 or $1,200. I think that would be harder than to spend an income of $50.000; at least it would give one far more headaches.
I do not think the treasury would lose very much if the minimum were set at $750 for single persons and SI,500 for married persons, making the national defence tax apply in the same way that the ordinary income tax applies. I really wish the minister would give this suggestion his consideration, because I am satisfied that w'hat he would lose in revenue we would gain in increased morale, increased good will and increased cooperation in carrying on this struggle.

A good deal of time has been spent on the discussion of resolutions 4 and 5, and I would not take up any more time but for the fact that I have something to say which may give the minister some satisfaction. I represent one of the largest constituencies in Canada. After this national defence tax was adopted during the last session of parliament. I spent most of my time in that constituency, where I had an opportunity of meeting and talking to some men and women in the lower income brackets. I also had an opportunity of talking to a great many others with whom I did not discuss this matter, but I did not meet one man or woman who complained about 
having to pay this tax. I believe they all took the view that it was only fair and right that they should make some direct contribution to the financing of this war; and although it is not pleasant to pay taxes, I believe they derived some satisfaction from the payment of this tax. Of course I do not know how they will feel about the increase that is being proposed, but I believe they will endeavour to meet it cheerfully and with good grace. One difficulty may develop later this year in connection with the additional deduction that will be made because of unemployment insurance. What the reaction will be I do not know, but so far as my constituency is concerned I believe, with a certain amount of assurance, that my people in the lower income brackets are glad to contribute in this way towards Canada's war effort.

I believe the majority of those in the higher income brackets would prefer to pay a greater tax in order that those in the lower income brackets might pay a little less. I think this measure would be improved if the minister would increase the tax on those in the low income bracket from two per cent to three per cent instead of from two per cent to five per cent, and at the same time increase the minimum from $660 to $700. I have not the same sympathy for the single person who has $700 to spend; I think he will still have sufficient money to see quite a few movies. I know $700 was about as much as I had to spend in three years when I was in the same position; nevertheless many of these people are endeavouring to own their own homes, and with the many other calls they have to meet, I believe the $700 minimum would be reasonable.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is a clerical error which should be corrected. The new rates proposed under resolution 4 are intended to come into effect on July 1, 1941, and it was proposed to change the minimum for the year beginning July 1, 1941. That is, the $600 limit is not being changed retroactively; that applies to the period from July 1, 1940, to July 1, 1941. and the $660 applies from that time on. As the resolution reads, that is not clear, and I think resolution 5 should be amended by adding the words "second half of the" after the words "for the", which would make the paragraph read:
5. That the amount of $600 mentioned in the national defence tax section be raised to $660 for the second half of the calendar year 1941 and for each year thereafter.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: I move accordingly.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.

Income War Tax Act

I wonder whether we may not get into further administrative difficulties as a result of this. When you file your annual income tax return you are on a calendar year basis, whereas in connection with this national defence tax you are on a half-year basis. Will it not cause further difficulty in compiling total income tax returns when the department has to compute the ordinary income tax on the calendar basis and then has to compute this tax on the half-year basis? It will be seen that there is a difference in the amount allowed for dependents after July 1, as compared with what there is now. Is there going to be any certainty as to what we shall do?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It will make more difficulties, but they are not impossible of solution. They can be worked out. There is nothing impossible about what is being proposed. It is just a change, that is all. The tax begins in the middle of the year.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It is making the intention clear.
But the exemptions are higher now than they were before. In other words, does a man with three children have exemption at the old rate, or the ne.v rate, or in between?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The matter of exemptions is worked out in resolution 6. When it is being discussed I can give the committee the way in which it is done.
Let us consider the case of a single worker who in the last six months of 1940 did not receive $300. Will he be entitled to a refund on all deductions made from his wages?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.
Should he then make his application immediately, and to whom?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He should write a letter to the commissioner of income tax, and when the forms are available-if they are not already available, and I do not believe they are-he will be sent forms to fill out.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
They will be sent to the employer.
Mr. O'NEILL: Just before six o'clock I was speaking to this resolution, and at that time I was given to understand that the intention behind the tax was, first, that of raising money. It was pointed out that there was a dire need for money, and that about $80,000,000 would be so raised. The second reason given was that it would curtail the consumption of those articles which might
have a tendency to create inflation in Canada. I am far from being satisfied with the tax in its present form, and certainly I am not satisfied with the explanation given.
I realize fully the necessity of raising money, and I have no objection at all to that. The working class in this country will pay, and they will pay with less complaining than will any other class. They always have done so, and they always will, not only in Canada but in any other country. The fact is that the working class make less complaints about taxation than do any other class; but there is such a thing as getting a tax to a point where it is eating into the very necessities of life. That, in my opinion, is what this tax is doing. If the government must raise the money, and if there is no other way in which it can be raised-and in passing let me say that I do not agree with that argument at all-if it wishes, it could add another one per cent to the taxation on the incomes of men like myself, and I am quite sure they would raise this $80,000,000. The government would then not have to place this burden on the shoulders of these people.
However, taking the argument that the government cannot get away from the tax, then I say that what it should do is this: Instead of taking the money as a tax, it should take it as a loan, and should put war savings certificates to the credit of these people while they are earning it. When the war is over, the money could be handed back to them. The government would have the use of the money while the war is on, just as it would have the money if it raised it by way of borrowing. For example, the government is going to raise a certain amount by the victory loan which will become operative on June 2. If this tax were done away with altogether, could the government not raise $680,000,000 instead of the $600,000,000 which it proposes to raise through the loan? I say it could be done, and by just the same means. If we really do not wish to take the money away from these people, then let us hold it in trust as war savings certificates until after the war. I believe these are suggestions which might be given due consideration.
Mr. O'BRIEN: Before six o'clock I spoke privately to the minister, asking him to clarify the situation with respect to the tax as it affects the piece-worker. In the lumbering industry of New Brunswick, and I have no doubt in other provinces, we have men working by the month on piece-work. They are paid by the cord. No doubt men in munitions and other plants are paid on a similar piece-
Income War Tax Act

work basis. Will the minister tell us if the tax should be deducted by the employer, or are such men treated as contractors?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If the piece-worker is an employee, the tax should be deducted. If he is an independent contractor, it should not. In that event he should make a return.
Mr. O'BRIEN:	How would we know
whether he is or is not? Does the law give any definition?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. It is just one of those things which must be decided by the employer himself. It is a very mild legal question, but not one about which it would be necessary to consult a solicitor.

I understood the minister to say that the exemption was S20 for each child. My reading of the resolution is that the exemption is only $14. I am not very familiar with these budgets. I have been through two budgets, and one baby budget. If I come back another year I shall have to bring a ton of hay and a cow to pay the rest of my income tax. However, my interpretation is that $20 is the exemption.
The hon. member for Kamloops, coming from British Columbia, has hit the nail on the head. It is absolutely impossible to feed, clothe and educate a child on $20; certainly it is not possible in British Columbia. Yet that is all the exemption allowed for children. As I understand the hon. member for Kamloops, the government would take the entire $60 over the $1,200 of a man earning $1,260. I believe it was the hon. member for Rose-town Biggar-I might even give the hon. member for Vancouver East credit for it- who pointed out last year that $48,000 was left to a man who had an income of $100,000. In other words, $52,000 was taken away from him. It was pointed out that the amount taken away was not important, he still had $48,000 left to live on.
As the hon. member for Kamloops pointed out, the minister suggested that if we were to add further taxation to these millionaires, and they are making plenty of money now; there is no doubt about that-we might disrupt their way of life. Surely it is disrupting the way of life when a stenographer right in this building is paying a national defence tax of $5. That is a tremendous tax to be imposed upon a stenographer. I believe it is So-hon. members can figure it out for themselves. The sessional stenographer receives $5 a day. When a man with a family is getting $1,200, immediately his tax goes up. So far, no provision has been made for the ordinary people.
There is one source of income which might be given further consideration-although I

do not know how much these people are already taxed. Does the government tax that dollar from the dollar-a-year men? They are still getting their salaries of $25,000 or $30,000 a year from their corporations. They must be receiving enough, receiving their $20 or $25 a day living allowance, that a tax would not have the effect of lowering their standard of living. On the other hand, a married man receiving $1,500 has to pay. It does not make any sense to me; I do not think it makes sense to anybody else, either. In my opinion, some consideration ought to be given to that fact.
As I said, the sessional stenographers receive approximately $5 a day. The national defence tax is a terrible one for such a girl or for a married man getting $1,200 to pay. I should, of course, like to see the exemption raised to above the sessional indemnity. Surely the minister should give some consideration to the suggestion which has been made by both sides of the house to raise the exemption. I think we have wasted too much time on this resolution already, and probably I am wasting more time because I do not think any attention is going to be paid to our representations. At the same time we represent the rank and file of the people of this country, not the millionaire class. I have not one millionaire in my riding, and never will have, because there is no chance of making big money there. The minister should take into consideration the representations that are made by members of parliament, representing the farmers, working men and the rank and file of the people of this country, rather than listen so much to recommendations from professional civil servants who have never tried to raise a family on $1,200 a year.

Before six
o'clock the hon. member for Rosedale and I asked the minister to have a computation made of the cost to the treasury if the exemption in the case of the national defence tax were raised to $750 for single people, and $1,400 for married people. Has the minister had that worked out?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have asked an official
of my department who, I thought, would be among those best qualified to give me the information, and he has given me this memorandum which I shall read. It is not very satisfactory because it is impossible to make an estimate with any definiteness at all:

Mr. COLDWELL; That breakdown is much more satisfactory. I do not think any one of us asks these questions out of mere curiosity but we wish to get a more accurate picture of the situation. I should like to have seen the twenty-seven broken down, but I express my appreciation of the minister's having brought this information down because in former years information as to incomes in the higher brackets has always been refused. Therefore I think we have made some progress this year in getting thus far.
I think if we were to have a free vote of this committee at the present time on these two resolutions we would find the majority of the committee in favour of raising the exemptions in the lower income brackets, and that being the situation, I think the minister and the government would be well advised to have these two resolutions stand in order that some consideration might be given to what appears to be a fairly general wish on the part of members of this committee. After all, this is a democratic country. It so happens, of course, that the government has an unusually large majority, but if we were more evenly balanced these two resolutions might be defeated. As it is, I think if a vote were taken now, the resolutions might have difficulty in getting through.
I realize that the minister has to raise the money, and like my colleague the hon. member for Vancouver East I recognize the ability with which the budget was brought down and the extent to which an endeavour was made to be fair; but like the hon. member for Lethbridge, while I know there is a necessity to transfer labour, material, machines and so on from peace-time industry to war-time industry, I do not believe that this is going to have that effect. If we have to transfer industry from one field to another, it seems to me it might be done directly rather than by resorting to means like this. I would much prefer to see some system of priorities put into effect, to cutting down the incomes of these lower-paid workers, and thereby compelling them, as the hon. member for Lethbridge said, to restrict their consumption of foodstuffs and clothing. We have in this country an abundance of food, and there is no need to reduce consumption. Indeed, to cut down food for the growing children of Canada will cause more war casualties, and of a different type, than those sustained on the field of battle, casualties which so far we have not had, and which, in any large number, I hope we may escape. The same process of cutting down will, as an hon. member reminds me, also have the effect of reducing the farmer's income.

I would say to the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) that, after all, we cannot compare the wages and salaries and earnings of thirty or forty years ago with the somewhat larger salaries which are being earned at the present time. Many things which have arisen since that time have now become necessities. When we speak of the humble movie, which is used so largely by people who can afford no other form of amusement, we must bear in mind that this very budget puts a twenty per cent tax on moving picture theatre tickets, and that is a substantial tax on those who enjoy that cheap forth of entertainment.

Would the hon. member
prefer to have a lower tax on single men and retain the higher tax on the married men?
Oh, no.
I was suggesting that we reduce the married men's bracket and retain the tax on the single men.

That is not the point
I was making. My point was this, that already we are taxing fairly substantially a luxury which the hon. member mentioned, and I do not believe that it enters into a consideration of these two resolutions. I believe that, if put to the vote of this committee at the present time, these resolutions would have great difficulty in carrying. As we have said, over and over again, it is not what the individual pays in taxes that counts, it is the amount that the individual has left. I maintain that these lower-paid groups, and particularly, if you will, the married group, will find it difficult to bear this tax, and I would rather see a slight increase in the taxes of, say, groups a little higher up, spread among them, to meet the deficit which the minister estimated a few minutes ago. speechtext:

feel like acceding to that very politely worded request. If anything like that is done, I shall have to resort to some other taxes. It may be that the committee is prepared to vote down this tax, but would they vote for a sales tax if I brought it in?
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, we are getting down to business when we are talking that way. The hon. gentleman says, "Spread it around among the higher incomes." But we have so few people there. We should also not forget

Perhaps it would not make much difference if you put them in a position where, without doing so, they could not pay their taxes. Does the minister think this tax is in the interests of the community?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We would not be doing any of this, of course, if it were not for the war.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is the answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But we are having to do it, and we are distributing it as fairly as we can. We can argue about that, but-

Where is the money for the big bond issue which is being talked about? The people in the $600 class are not going to be able to buy bonds.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, no, I suppose they
are not.

important question. speechtext: We have not come yet to the capital levy, and I do not think we shall come to it. I must say that, while I have heard the capital levy advocated, I have not seriously considered it.

speechtext: Yes. Many people who buy bonds are going to buy them out of capital.

May I say a word in this connection? I believe the minister realizes that so far as our party is concerned, we want to cooperate with him in every way possible. We know that he must raise the money, and we are willing to do anything we can to help him to do it. But I do feel, in view of the figures he gave to-night, that it would be a matter of somewhere between $13 and $20 million-

I realize that it is just an estimate. But if we were to levy the taxes in some places where I think they should be levied, I believe these exemptions could be raised. As I stated on the budget debate, there are people who are in a position to pay $3 for a dinner, $5 to hear a symphony concert, and SI to $2.50 to see a hockey match-all of which ma3' be classed as absolute luxuries which the average person cannot afford, and which the people in the low income-tax brackets who will be affected by these increases of from two to five and from three to seven per cent, cannot pay; yet, as a House of Commons, we are making no attempt to tax this type of luxury, and the people who can afford these luxuries are going scot-free. I suggest that, under this resolution, we exempt the single and married people, and levy a substantial tax on these other luxurious indulgences which have not been taxed under the act; I believe that we could raise thereby a substantial amount of money. If people insist on enjoying these luxuries at a time when the minister is trying to stop inflation and stop unnecessary spending, let them pay. The only reason why they enjoy them is because they have the money to do so.
