Income War Tax Act

I do not wish to hold up these resolutions, but do many hon. members realize how painfully this tax will hurt certain people? This is precisely the standard of salary that affects thousands upon thousands of young people, schoolteachers. I have been a schoolteacher, and I know something of what they have to go through. If a young teacher gets $660 a year and receives $10 a year increase, which is a fairly substantial increase in the rural areas of the three prairie provinces and perhaps British Columbia, may I point out that the teacher paying this tax would have to teach three solid years and get no effective increase at all, because she can get no money beyond the $660 until she gets up to $694.75. That is because the government is taking everything over $660.
Some people have asked the question, where will you get the money? Go into the Chateau Laurier; go into the Fort Garry; go into the Macdonald, any of the high class hotels, and gaze upon the lordly creatures who keep their heads in the air, and roam up and down the corridor. Those are the people who can afford to pay money. Those people who are getting $660 a year never go and buy a sixty cent meal, but there are plenty of well-to-do people who go and get a meal for a dollar and twenty-five cents. Why not put a tax on meals above sixty cents? There you are getting at luxuries. Why not put a definite tax on all hotel rooms above $2? There is no one in the country who cannot sleep in complete comfort in a $2 room, yet there are people who occupy high-priced rooms while we are taxing young people who have to go and hunt up a twenty-five cent or a fifty cent bed, stealing into a room upstairs in some Chinese-
Joss house.

-restaurant, in order to get by. We members do not know the meaning of these things; that is all. We do not know where the pressure is being put on. Look at the people who occupy chair cars, parlour cars, special compartments on the train. Look at any big transcontinental train and see how many people there are occupying these compartments. Why not make them pay extra? All these things are luxuries. Take membership in expensive clubs. The men who can afford to go and play golf in the big country clubs, the Mayfairs and whatnot, can afford to pay. There is no objection to their playing golf there, but the people who are patronizing these organizations can afford to pay. They are spending the money now. They are spending money that most of our young people will never dream of spending.

Let me give a picture of the young schoolteacher-and we must not overlook this. The young schoolteacher has to pay her way, and most of these teachers are girls, although there are some boys. They have to pay $25 or $30 to reach the place where they are to teach. They have to pay their return fare if they wish to spend their Christmas or Easter holidays at home. What a hole that makes in their income! While some of them are able to get room and board for $20, many will have to pay $30. There is no allowance for that in this tax, which is a blanket tax. It makes no difference what condition they are in, they will have to pay the tax. The schoolteacher has to keep herself in clothes; she has to pay for laundry, and she has to buy various necessities. Then, she often wants to go to summer school; she may have to pay back a loan of $200 or $300. What chance has she? This tax is simply tragically inequitable when you consider those who are enjoying real luxuries in comparison with these young people.
I know there is going to be a great deal of disinclination to take seriously what I now say, but I will say it nevertheless, and say it freely. Between 1914 and 1917 the dominion government created $26,000,000 of bills and used that money in defraying government expenses. Let no man rise in his place in this house and say that there is no other way of getting money than by taxation. If hon. members wish to read about that creation-I will not elaborate-I refer them to a pamphlet which is to be found in the library. It is the report of the royal commission on banking and currency in Canada, 1933, and the procedure will be found set out at page 22, paragraph 47. There is no laughing that off; it is there, because it occurred. The reason why I asked the minister so carefully about inflation was this. If anything had been said about that transaction four years ago, the then Minister of Finance would have risen in a semi-frenzied state and shouted "inflation." I happened to be here, and saw him do it. The point is we have discovered now that that could not cause inflation, because the expenditure of a million dollars of that created money would have no more effect on prices than a million dollars raised or obtained in any other way, especially if the latter were taken from people who would not otherwise spend it. I am not going to elaborate the matter, but the minister might just as well get ready to take this step sooner than later because he must take it. For him to bring down here year after year a set of taxes so burdensome as this, which I know it pains him as much as us, to put on, is simply not sound, and it must not go on.

Income War Tax Act
I think I have said enough on that. I wish to raise just one more point, and then, so far as I am concerned, I am going to let this resolution go through without saying any more. With respect to these commodities of which there is danger of a shortage, has the minister set up any machinery whereby he may know what commodities we are in danger of running short of? Is it any one of the fruits: strawberries, currants, gooseberries, raspberries, plums, peaches, pears or apples? Is it any of the vegetables? Is it potatoes? Is it any one of the grains? Is it any of the grain products? Is it any dairy product? Is it any of the meats? Is it wool? Is it clothing? While we are speaking of clothing, hon. members will recall that in the last war we were beginning to run short of clothes at about this stage of the war; people were not able to get the kind of clothes they were accustomed to. Several times since this war started, the clothing dealers have got all ready for a rise in prices and begun to talk about how they could not procure these particular clothes any more, but they have got over that and have now begun to advertise sales because they could not sell, which indicates that there is no shortage of clothes.
There are, however, scores and scores of other commodities as to which when we ask, is there danger of a shortage? the answer must be "no". There must be still other commodities of which there is danger of a shortage. Has the minister set up machinery to find out what they are? If not, why not? Why not go at this matter in a scientific way; why not do our housekeeping on business principles? Let us know where we stand. I do not think anyone is going to buy a car if there is danger of inflation or impairment of Canada's war effort thereby, although cars are becoming almost a necessity for many people nowadays. People are not going to buy radios or other specific commodities if they realize that they would be thereby doing a disservice to Canada. And if they persist, let us ration them and say that in a given area we will allow only so many radios or cars to be sold.
Mr. HOMUTH; If you rationed them, to whom would you give them?

We rationed things in the last war. They rationed sugar; I know that on many occasions they decided they would not give me sugar. They had no trouble in deciding with regard to me. They actually began rationing flour also. If I remember correctly, there was only a certain kind one could get.
But everyone got some.
Do not pay any attention to him.

Yes, he is talking good sense this evening. If there is really a shortage so that you have to ration, I suppose you will have to draw lots. But surely the minister could find experts to advise him as to ways to distribute. Surely we do not have to tax these young school teachers in the country to the point where they can hardly dress themselves decently and can not possibly save $20; we do not have to do that to keep anyone from buying a car.
Mr. O'NEILL: At the risk of incurring the displeasure of the Minister of Finance and perhaps the whip, I should like to ask if consideration could be given to changing the amount collected by this national defence tax to a loan repayable after the war. If consideration cannot be given to that, what are the objections?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman puts
quite a burden upon me when he asks me to go into this question of forced loans and the level at which they should start. In England they have a system of forced loans, but I think they take more in taxes than we do out of these very income groups, and then they start on their loans after that. Perhaps I have not thought through this question of loans as thoroughly as I should have. I dealt with it to some extent this afternoon. I think the hon. gentleman was present at the time. It would occur to me, however, that the time would come when we had to repay this money, and it might be at a time when it would be difficult to raise it. People would demand the money; they would not want to renew or refund the amount. A great task of financing would be put upon us at that stage. We might be in a period of deflation when it would be very difficult for the government to raise large sums of money. We could not agree to repay all that we take from the people in taxes, somewhere between $1,000,000,000 and $1,400,000,000. That might be very desirable from the point of view of individuals after the war; they would be happy to be getting their money back, but from whom would we get the money with which to pay them?
Tax them over again.
From the Bank of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have to keep some of the money we take. I am not prepared now at any rate to start making people give us money by way of loans.

After listening for the best part of two days to this discussion, I have come to the conclusion that we have wasted a great deal of time, that we are not going
Income I For Tax Act

to get any changes in this item. I would remind the committee that so long as the people of this country and many hon. members in this house are satisfied that our resources shall be used on the basis of profits instead of human needs, the Minister of Finance is going to be placed in the position he is in to-day. He must play the game according to the rules. He -must get the money to finance the war and he must do it in this way so long as we are satisfied with the rules that guide him.
With respect to this tax on incomes of $660, I do not consider it a tax, I consider it a crime. Fifty-five dollars a month is not an income. No one can live on it.
Many do.

I am not much concerned about raising the exemption to S750 because it still would be away below a decent standard of living. I do not think anyone with an income under 81,200 should bo taxed, and sixty-five per cent of the working people of this country have an income under $1,200. T think that should be the exemption. I am, however, pretty sure we are not going to get it at this time.
I am prepared to assist the Minister of Finance, and I think this group is, in going in the other direction so far as it is possible to go, with respect to raising the funds necessary to prosecute the war. You can take away something from the income groups above SI,500 without pulling them down to where it means a shortage of the necessities of life. They have something to give; and I think if we intend to do the job as it should be done, everyone in this country should come to the point where they are really making some sacrifice. If I have an income of $10,000 a year and the actual necessities of life can be obtained for $1,500, if you take everything I have above $1,500, I am still not making any sacrifice. I am not suffering; I have enough to eat and enough to wear, and I am not going into debt. I think that is the way we should work.
Within the last few weeks I have seen much in the newspapers and heard a great deal on the street with regard to unrest among labour, strikes, stoppages of work and so on. Well, we have the answer to that in the discussion which has taken place during the last two days. The answer is that sixty-five per cent of the working people of this country receive less than 81,200 a year. Since the outbreak of war we have added a great many indirect taxes which have increased the cost of living by perhaps twenty-five per cent. In addition, we have war savings certificates, which are practically compulsory so far as the average
[Mr. Gillis.l
worker is concerned. Then there have been drives for war services, the Red Cross, and so on, to which all the workers have been asked to contribute. I do not think twenty-five per cent of the ordinary people understand the reason for the lowering of their standard of living. These things are being taken from them insidiously, and they do not understand it. The natural reaction is to try to get back what they are losing. They understand that it is much harder to get along; they are working longer hours and more man-days per week, and it is only natural that they should seek to replace what they appear to be losing.
That is the reason for the unrest, and the euro is so to order your finances that you do not tax those who are unable to make any sacrifice, that you do not drive people below the subsistence level. When you tax that sixty-five per cent of the common people who receive low incomes; when you reduce them below the subsistence level, then you sow the seeds of communism and everything that goes with it, because you are actually threatening their very existence and most of them do not understand it. Personally I think we would be well advised, if a change is necessary, to fix the minimum amount necessary for a reasonable standard of living at around $1,200 or $1,500, and take everything that anyone has above that. If anyone is not prepared to do this he is not interested in prosecuting this war and fighting the machine that is going to clamp down on us if we do not win. Lip-service is not good enough; a practical demonstration is needed. I think Clement Attlee very well stated the case in the British House of Commons when he told the British people that without the full application of socialist principles in the prosecution of the war, we could not win. I believe Ernest Bevin struck the right note when he said, "When you allow dissension and distrust to creep into the minds of the peace army, the army of working people who produce the sinews of war, then you are going to lose the war."
That is what we are doing when we impose these burdens on those who are below the subsistence level at the present time. We call it taxing them, but these are not taxes. I think every member of this group, and perhaps every member of this house, are prepared to make some real sacrifice. We should start tightening our belts, stop driving our cars, and begin giving what we have above what it costs to live. These people in the income group below $1,200 have not enough on which to live; and if a man has $40,000 or 810,000 or even 85,000 left, no one can say he is making any sacrifice, for he is not. Over in Britain

Income War Tax Act
they are living underground; they have given everything they owned. Their homes are smashed up; in one city fifty thousand people were forced into the fields with nowhere to sleep. They are in the front line of the battle for freedom; but over here we say we are making a sacrifice when we still have something left. We are doing no such thing. That is why there is so much chaos and unrest among the working people of Canada to-day. Too many people at the top are standing pat, holding on to what they have. Too many people in this house and outside it are prepared to have the country run under the rules now in force, with profits overriding human needs. I do not know of anyone who could do a better job than the minister, while conforming to the rules, but I think it is time we started changing those rules. Talking about it is not good enough; the people must be given a demonstration. I am prepared to assist in taking everything above $1,200 or $1,500. Let us get down to where we are all making some sacrifice; then we can go out and do a job with the people.

It seems to me that we are at cross-purposes. Is the object of this tax to raise revenue, or is it to keep down consumption? Some hon. members seem to believe the only money the government can get is that money which it taxes from the pockets of the people. If that be so, we have no option but to increase taxation to the point where large numbers of people will be literally starved to death. We know, however, that is not the situation. As I mentioned this afternoon, in Great Britain they get all they can by taxes, and they borrow all they can; yet they are spending something like two thousand million pounds a year in addition. In other words the government or the banks are creating ten thousand million dollars a year in addition to what they tax and what they borrow.
If the object of this tax is to keep down inflation by curtailing consumption, there are other ways of preventing inflation than by bringing about unnecessary suffering on the part of those people in the lower income brackets. I do not believe the prosecution of this war will be helped by lowering the standard of living of any people below what is necessary to keep up their strength, health and morale. There might be a system of rationing, as some hon. members have mentioned already. In Great Britain they have been following for some time the principle of compensating prices; that is, in connection with some essential foods and other commodities the retailers are authorized to sell at less than cost, and then they are compensated to the extent that they are out of
pocket. I am not going to say that this is the social credit principle, because if I did, the suggestion would meet with great opposition, but that principle has been adopted in Britain, I believe to the extent of half a billion dollars a year.
The point I wish to make, if I can, is that we should be clear in our minds as to the precise object of this tax. Is it for the simple purpose of raising revenue, or is it to cut down consumption? I think the minister will agree that it is principally for the latter purpose, but I suggest that there are better methods of controlling inflation than by reducing the standard of living of perhaps hundreds of thousands of people in this country below what is necessary to preserve their health and their morale.

I was hoping the minister would reply to the question raised by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin. It seems to me that the minister has fallen into the error into which former ministers fell, namely, that he is contradicting himself in connection with this matter. He stated emphatically, in reply to the hon. member for Parry Sound, that the idea was not that of stopping these people from spending their $600. And yet, on two occasions in this house he has stressed the fact that the taxation is not merely for the purpose of providing revenue but also to curtail spending. He made that statement most emphatically.
I have in my hand a statement by Professor Plumptre, who says:
It _ must be remembered primarily, and seemingly paradoxically, that the government's object is not to get money but merely to reduce the public's spending. The government can always get money, because it may, as an alternative to borrowing or even to taxation, create the required funds.
The statement made by the minister is in direct conflict with that which he has made in the house on previous occasions.
Let us for the moment examine the minister's statement that the tax is not for the purpose of preventing spending. If it is merely for the purpose of raising revenue- and apparently that is what it is for; it is not to curtail spending-would the minister suggest that the people in the $600 limit are in a position to provide that revenue? I think he has admitted that they are not. They are also now suffering certain hardships. I suggest then that we should tax the people who are going to buy bonds. The minister has stated that that would be in the form of a levy, and that it could not be met out of current revenue.
Then, according to the minister's own admission, neither the poor nor the rich are

Income War Tax Act
in a position to pay taxes higher than those imposed at the present time. If the people's spending has been reduced to as low a level as we dare reduce it, then I would suggest that the logical place to get money would be from the Bank of Canada, because such a condition would show that we have not too much money in circulation. And if the government is still going to continue to refuse to use that method, although reference is made to it by Professor Plumptre, then I would go back to the other idea, namely, that if we had to do it by taxation, then certainly there are more equitable ways than that of increasing the taxation against the people who come within the $600 limit.
I would say that there are very few hon. members who are making any real sacrifice at the present time. I am quite satisfied that the tax on members of parliament could very easily be raised, and it would be far better to raise the tax on them than to raise it upon the people who are within the S600 limit. Further, if the minister will introduce an amendment to that effect, I shall support it immediately.
Take it all.

A very large sum of money could be raised from the people who have taxable incomes of from $3,000 to $5,000, and I do not see why it would not be possible to increase taxation on that class, rather than increase it on those in the $600 limit.
Why not let the members come here for nothing?
Members, like everybody else, would have something to live for. They are in a preferred position, some having high incomes from other sources.
No, they are not. You just said, "Soak the members"!
I say: Increase the taxation against members, rather than against those in the $600 limit.
Take it all, then.

The people in the $7,000 a year or $5,000 a year class can certainly stand higher taxation than the people within the $600 limit. There are a large number of taxis which come to the door, driving members around. I suggest it would do the members good to walk for a change. It would not hurt them a bit. That is one place where they could save money.
If I waited for taxis I would not be here more than once a month.
There are more equitable ways of raising this taxation.

Mr. Chairman, I had not expected to say anything, but it seems to me that the point raised concerning the lowest amount upon which this tax is payable, and the remarks of the hon. member for Parry Sound, and other hon. members, make it necessary for me to add my 'mice.
This is our second year of war, and we are told on all sides that we may expect a long period of government expenditures, and increasing government taxes, to meet the cost of the war as we go along. I am one who is concerned'-and I have no doubt we all are- not only with the progress of this war, its financial aspects, and other points in connection therewith, but also as to conditions in Canada when the war is over. It seems to me clear that the minister wants so far as possible to cause saving by those whose incomes are being raised, due to the enormous expenditure of government funds during the progress of the war. It is only natural that the minister should want that saving, because so far as possible he wishes to withdraw that money from circulation.
It seems to me, however, that one should look a little beyond that, and seek to get the people to save in order that they, themselves, may be protected in that hour when the war is over. I have sat in the house for a short time, and I have heard hon. members to my left, and also those on the government side, demanding from time to time that the old age pension should be raised. From the point of view of the amount of money an old age pensioner has to live on, I entirely agree. But from the other point of view, namely, that of paying moneys out of the consolidated revenue fund, paying millions of dollars extra each year, with no contra collections, then I think such a procedure would be hardly feasible.
With that in mind I should like to leave a thought with the minister. Let me say clearly that I consider this amount too low. Let there be no misunderstanding about that. I would, however, be prepared to support any motion made by the minister or the government, between now and the next session, to introduce legislation of a contributory nature-compulsory, if you wish; preferably compulsory- whereby all employed persons would contribute

Income War Tax Act
a percentage monthly of their pay cheques, such moneys to go to a fund which, if necessary, the government might use during the war for war purposes. Then, when the war is over, these amounts would be paid back to persons who had reached a certain required age-possibly sixty, or whatever might be stipulated. There we would have a pension upon which such persons could live, without work.
I recollect bitterly the years from 1932, onward. Hon. members know I speak the truth when I say it was evident to all who in any way were connected with employment throughout Canada-and particularly with unemployment-that between 1932 and 1936 there was not enough work in Canada to go round, so as to give our young people a chance to work.
Why stop at 1936?

I shall not argue about that. If any hon. member has anything to say, he will have an opportunity to say it. I have one thought in the back of my head, one which I believe a good many people have, including some in the army. We do not want to go back to that again. But if we do not set aside some moneys so that we can take some people off the labour market when the war is over, then I say we are going to have the same bad state of employment. And, on the financial side, we shall have to redeem issues of bonds, war savings certificates in a large measure, all of which will mean heavy taxation and low employment.
Why can we not now make provision for a scheme similar, so far as collection is concerned, to the unemployment insurance scheme? If a person were out of work he would not have to forgo his rights, because the unemployment insurance scheme could be tied in. I do not need to tell the committee what is being done in the United States, because I am sure hon. members know that very well.
I feel strongly, however, that if we are going to take a few dollars off the pay of the working people in this country, then we should take it off and say at the same time, "This money is going to be placed in a fund, and when you reach a certain age you will get a certain pension. It will not be something for nothing, and there is no charity about it. You will have laid aside for it, and it will be paid back to you."
In this way-and I suggest this in all sincerity-we will remove a feeling of insecurity from the minds of a great many people, who are to-day about forty-five or fifty years of
age and who, when this war is over, will certainly not have a chance on the labour market. I do not know of any better way of keeping up their morale in this struggle than by removing that fear of insecurity. This is only a suggestion. I have neither the time nor the knowledge to go very much further at the moment, but the Minister of Finance has his experts, as has also the Minister of Labour. I feel most strongly that if a certain portion of the tax went into a pension fund, the government would have a very much better response and that such action would be definitely in the public interest.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Think of the next generation.

I would ask the Minister of Finance to think of next year and the year after. We are in the most destructive conflict the world has ever seen. We are in a battle to the death which is going to test the powers and resources of every man, woman and child in Canada, as well as the natural resources of this dominion. We must, of course, achieve victory at any cost. I have listened to a discussion about raising the exemptions above .$660 and other figures. We must win this war if it takes all we have, and the main question before us as members of parliament is not how this may please some group of labour men or some group of manufacturers or some group of financial interests, but how we can best preserve what might be termed the goose that lays the golden egg. How can we preserve our resources to last through a war that shows no sign of being ended in 1941 and possibly not in 1942 or 1943 or 1944, and perhaps not in 1945? It is more likely to be 1946 before this terrible conflict will end.
I am not so much concerned about the taxes we are paying this year. What I am concerned about is, shall we win if you take everything we have in 1945? This conflict is so serious that our people have not grasped its significance even yet, and I say that in all seriousness. It is not a question of whether you should take ten per cent or more this year. It is a question whether we can win if we give everything we have in 1945. Look at the headlines in the papers. Do not get alarmed about Hess flying over to Britain. Look at the possibility of France [Mr. Hsley.l
joining the enemy, and of Russia possibly lining up with the axis, and Japan with her. The challenge is clearly before us, and we must plan for a long-range effort, and if we can plan so that we can maintain this rate of taxation, then I say that this rate of taxation is not too high. But when one considers many of these taxes, one must consider what effect they are going to have not only on the individual but on the industries involved.
Referring to resolutions 8, 9 and 10, I compliment the minister upon having removed one discriminatory feature of the original proposal. To my mind it was ridiculous to suggest for one moment that because some company had planned for its bonds and interest to be paid in United States funds, those payments should be exempt, while payments of another company, which perhaps in a more or less haphazard way had arranged to pay in Canadian funds, should not be exempt. I can well remember Premier Hepburn in the last provincial campaign in Ontario stating that henceforth Ontario bonds would be paid in Canadian funds, and he criticized arrangements which had been made in the past to pay in, United States funds. Had this clause stood as drafted originally, it would have been most unfair to the province of Ontario. Why should we say that the United States bondholder who holds Dominion of Canada bonds should not be taxed fifteen per cent, while United States bondholders who hold province of Ontario bonds payable in Canadian funds should be taxed fifteen per cent? I am glad the minister has eliminated that provision.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think the hon.

Just the opposite of what the hon. member said.

Anyway, I am glad to be

I have no objection to the five per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Will the hon. gentleman
permit me to intervene at this stage? It is just the proper stage to clear up what I think is a misapprehension. The hon. gentleman has referred to the high taxes which residents of the United States will have to pay as they progressively participate in war production. Let me make it clear that a resident of the United States of America may deduct from the income tax which he pays to the United States government in respect of this income which he derives from the Dominion of Canada, the tax which we are levying on him by this resolution. That is, if his income tax is as high as or higher than fifteen per cent on this income, he simply pays it to the Canadian government instead of to the United States government and is not any worse off.

Insurance companies in the
United States of America do not pay any income tax, and many of these bonds are held by those companies. I am, I believe, just as conscious as is the minister of his requirements in the way of revenue, and I believe I am just as sincere as any other hon. member in looldng upon this matter from the long-range point of view of strengthening our ability to pay. If you do not take the money this year you will take it next year; and before this war is over, I believe our payments will be far larger than any we are criticizing or suggesting to-night. Someone has talked about the taxing of the $660 a year men. Some other hon. member spoke of taking half the incomes of the $20,000 a year men, but the government will take three-fourths of it before this war is over, and we shall be glad to give it in order to win the victory which now at times looks difficult. I am as convinced that we shall win this war as I am of my own existence, but we shall win it only by every man, woman and child in this country, irrespective of politics, getting behind the Minister of Finance and behind the government.
There are many things I should like to say to the government with the object of saving at least part of that eighty million dollars. I am concerned, for instance, about some of the lawns which are being laid, at a cost of hundreds of thousands of dollars, in front of officers' messes across this country. I am concerned over some other extravagances. But I am not going to make an issue of these matters, because there is a far bigger picture which demands all our attention, which makes us feel that we are all in this battle, and, whether we like it or not, we must smother all party and racial prejudices and all religious bias, and realize that this great British country, Canada, is fighting alongside the motherland for the survival of freedom itself. We must rise far above the little, petty criticisms of matters which affect us politically and financially. I am as convinced of that as I am that there is a God above.
But I repeat, what I have said privately to the minister, that I would be very careful not to sap the very root and vitality of our financial strength. And I say to my hon. friends of the left that if the labour men of this country are to receive the high standard of living which is their desire and ours, we must protect the capitalistic fabric of this country.

Capitalism goes hand-inhand with democracy.
Hear, hear.

I am glad to hear my hon. friend say, "hear, hear." If you destroy the capitalist system and the initiative which seeks and deserves reasonable remuneration for its services, you will destroy not only the goose which lays the golden eggs, but the hopes of the labour men of this country.
That is right.

My hon. friend says, "that
is right." I am glad to hear him say so.
At $660 a year!

May I tell my hon. friend
that I have paid men on my farm $660 a year who have had far less worries than I had, and who in fact looked more prosperous than either he or I do at present. We have a different status, different places, in the social fabric of this country. Do not let us get too soft-hearted. The hour has struck when we must look these issues squarely in the face. We must not talk primarily for the satisfaction of some hired man on my farm or anywhere else, some man with an income of $600 or $700 a year, living along a brook-trout stream in a house renting at $5 a month, who can live more happily than some of my hon. friends who have not paid their Chateau Laurier accounts for the last three months. I shall not mention any names, although I see an hon. member who, I think, paid his last night.

Do not look at me,
because I do not stay there.

I say this in all seriousness: I have rented houses at $4 a month to men with happy families, with better houses than some hon. members in urban districts are living in at $40 a month. So do not let us get confused by these references to $660. I have seen men in the rural districts, in 1932 and 1933, too proud to take relief, men who had fought in the last great war; but they kept their chins up and said, "We will see it through." I have in mind one man who lived on $20 a month and kept nine children. Four of them are to-day fighting in his majesty's forces overseas and they are still happy.
Does the hon. member think it is a disgrace to live on relief?

I do not think so, and if I had to do so I would, rather than die. But this man was too proud to live on relief, and he

said he could survive on that amount. The man for whom he was working would give him a few bags of potatoes, but he did survive and he saw it through. I say, therefore, do not suggest that a man with $660 in certain districts cannot survive. As every hon. member knows, I have fought for the labourer as much as anyone else has done.
It is not equality of sacrifice when one has $600 and the other $60,000.

No, probably not; but the man with $600 never aspired to have $60,000, and the man with $60,000 would possibly be happy if he had the $600 and did not have the responsibility involved in the other amount. Do not let us grow soft on this. Let us face the issue. I have every sympathy for the Minister of Finance, but I should like to give him this warning: Be careful lest you dry up the source from which you get the vital, fundamental necessities to win this war; because it is not the taxes of 1940 or 1941, it is not the taxes of 1942 that we have to consider, but Canada's ability to maintain her financial structure and to keep her economic resources sound against the days of 1945 and 1946, so as to meet all the difficulties which we shall have to go through before the war is won. Let us, therefore, face the storm with our chins up and not turn our backs to the enemy because of political opportunism and the expediency of the hour.

Resolution 10 brings up a question which I would ask the minister to consider. It provides for an increase of from five to fifteen per cent on non-resident persons in respect of the total amount of royalties, rentals or similar payments for use in Canada of patents, real or personal property-and it is these words with which I am directly concerned-or for anything used or sold in Canada. In western Canada there is quite a lot of British capital invested in buildings, perhaps office buildings, homes, and so on. This tax is a tax on gross rental. It makes no allowance for taxes that have to be paid to the municipality, for the cost of collecting rentals, for insurance or repairs to these buildings; and in some instances the result has been that after the tax has been paid, the whole amount of the rental has been eaten up and the owner has had to advance money from some other source. In other words, it has become a capital tax. I suggest to the minister that at least a bottom should be put to the tax and that it should not apply below net income. If you take the whole of the net income, that is one thing; but to go further and make a man pay capital is entirely unfair.

It is not the type of tax that should be imposed by this House of Commons. The British owner is in the position where he may have to pay from his capital, while next door the Canadian owner has a building on which he pays income tax only on net rentals received. That is an unfair situation, and at the very least we should not tax more than net rental.

This tax on gross was designed to effect rough justice, and doubtless does. In a great many instances it probably is not as heavy a tax as a forty per cent rate on the net profits would be. If, however, any foreign owner wishes to be treated exactly the same as his Canadian competitor, all he has to do is to incorporate and then he will be a Canadian resident, get rid of this entirely and pay the same rate as the Canadian competitor.

The Canadian owner does not have to incorporate, so he would not be treated the same. At the present time, in some instances you are taxing capital; it is not an income tax at all. I suggest that that is not fair.

I should like to commend the minister for increasing this rate of tax from five to fifteen per cent. I do not propose to enter into an argument with the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe regarding the merits and demerits of the capitalist system, but I think it should be clear to all that those who have invested money in Canada have an interest in the outcome of the present conflict. Our victory is their victory. Should defeat come, it will be their loss. It is only fair that those who have made any form of investment should bear their fair share of the cost.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I must admit that in the
first place I could not see any difference in principle between taxing bond interest which was payable in Canadian funds on bonds held by non-resident owners and bond interest payable in United States funds on bonds held by non-resident owners. It was due to my inexperience perhaps that I did not see it, because, whether my reasoning was sound or unsound, it is undoubtedly considered by everybody who deals in bonds-banks, trust companies, insurance companies, certainly in the United States-that there is a difference. They consider that when Canadian provinces, municipalities or corporations go into the New York money market and offer bonds payable in United States funds in New York, there is an implied obligation on the part of Canadian authorities not to impose taxes on those payments. They consider that we have gone into their money market and floated our securities and agreed to pay them so many dollars in their own currency.
It was represented to me by ever so many persons that the situation was not the same at all with regard to securities payable in our own currency, that they would regard that as an internal matter subject to the changes in conditions that we might meet from time to time. After I heard a number of these representations, many by gentlemen who were most considerate, most friendly, and who appeared to be as anxious as we are to advance the war effort of Canada, I was convinced that it would be injurious to the credit of Canada if we continued that provision. In 1933, Mr. Rhodes who was then, I think, Minister of Finance, undertook to do the same thing, perhaps for the same reasons, and he also withdrew it. But I intend to withdraw the rest of the clause, because I think our securities that are payable in Canadian funds and are now in the hands of United States holders, whether they be provincial or municipal or corporation securities, should have their interest taxed now at a higher rate.
Hon. gentlemen must realize that the United States rate against non-residents is 164 per cent. That is subject to the convention or agreement between the United States and Canada which was made in 1936, by which that rate was reduced to five per cent both ways. With the imposition of this fifteen per cent rate, that convention lapsed and they will tax us at 164 per cent and we will tax them at 15 per cent, which is fairly even. The reason why I think we are justified, and I do not think it will be resented abroad to any extent is this. Of course some holders of these bonds, like insurance companies and

mutual organizations of one kind or another who are not subject to income tax and who, therefore, will not be able to set off this increase against the income taxes which they pay the United States government, will be out a little on this. But in my view they should share the fortunes of the Canadian people with regard to taxation on income which has its origin in Canada. We are taxing our own people fifteen per cent on the first $1,000 of that taxable income, in addition to the national defence tax. We have not touched the five per cent rate all these years; we have not moved this non-resident rate up' until we have taxed our own people very, very heavily. It would appear to me to be just, and I think in retrospect at least it will be regarded as just by everyone, to have this rate raised from five per cent to fifteen per cent.

speechtext: Yes, locally. We sell bonds to our own people, signed by us, and then we turn round and take as much as fifty per cent or ninety per cent out of the interest on those very bonds for which we promise to pay.
It would be no worse than doing it to Ontario bonds.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, I should be embarrassed if I were waited upon by persons who had bought our bonds and said, "We bought your bonds, and then after we got your bonds you got some of the money."

You would be embarrassed; but the premier of Ontario is embarrassed;
that is the difference.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, it is a different matter. This principle is well established. It has been established for eight years.

Resolution 9 deals with the tax applicable to non-resident-owned investment corporations. In his budget speech the minister did not deal with this tax, and I am wondering whether he could give us an estimate of the amount he hopes to realize by the increase from 9 per cent to 22^ per cent, and also a statement as to how much was realized out of this 9 per cent tax in the last fiscal period.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What has been received under the 9 per cent rate, and what will be received under the 22J per cent rate?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The amount assessed in the fiscal year 1940-41 on these non-resident-owned investment corporations was $842,810.95. That amount might not all have been for that year. It might relate to a previous year or previous years. But that was the amount assessed in that year. What was the other question the hon. member asked?
I should like to have an estimate as to how much it is expected will be raised in consequence of the increase to 22J per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No estimate was made.
It would be 250 per cent increase, would it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The amount would depend upon various things. They might not continue in business.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Has there been any protest against this tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

There is one element I wanted to point out to the minister, one which of course he realizes, namely, that these nonresident-owned investment companies will in all probability not continue in business. I believe the committee probably knows that these are companies which came to Canada, and which were created in this country for the purpose of holding investments here belonging to non-residents. They came here because they got in Canada the security of our laws, and they had confidence in our institutions. For these reasons some hundreds of millions of dollars of capital were brought here from Europe, the United Kingdom and the United States. A good deal of that money has since left Canada for the United States. But there is a great deal left here yet.
I suggest that the committee and the minister ought seriously to consider whether or not the amount he hopes to get from this increased tax is worth the loss to Canada which would arise from the money ultimately leaving the country. I suggest that if the tax is imposed it will be in the interests of owners of the companies either to dissolve them and remove the assets out of Canada, if they can, or just to dissolve them and to put the assets in custodian accounts in Canada, in which even the Canadian government would lose almost all of the tax it is now receiving.
I suggest that if this 22-j per cent tax is imposed, at the first opportunity which presents itself these owners of capital will remove that capital from the country, and that it will not come back. They placed the money here on investment, because they had confidence in our institutions. They felt it would be secure in this country, and they acted with the assurance that they would be well and favourably treated throughout the years, so far as taxation is concerned. A substantial business was built up from the very fact that people throughout the world had confidence in Canada. This business was a mark of the feeling of security felt by the investing world in the future of Canada and in its institutions. When we begin to destroy the basis of that confidence, by imposing a tax such as the one now proposed, we are taking a most important move.
I share with hon. members our sense of responsibility, and our sympathy with and confidence in the minister. I share with them

our desire to help him in every possible way to raise the vast sums of money required. In fact, I believe even the owners of the capital here involved would like to contribute, provided such contributions did not make it impossible for them to derive any benefit whatsoever from the continuance of their investments in Canada. But I seriously raise the question as to whether this is not getting out of line with what the traffic will bear; I am wondering if by such a tax the future of the country will best be served.
I would recall to the minds of hon. members that when this tax was first imposed it stood at 2\ per cent over the tax on non-residents. That amount was considered by our government and those responsible for taxation to be a proper charge upon these companies for the benefits and privileges of acquiring jurisdiction in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not quite that.
That was my information. It was a rough charge, arrived at in that way; and it was considered that that was what it was worth to these companies.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: How far back does it go?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I believe it was 1936 or 1937.
It would be 1936, I should think.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Then it cannot be loaded on to the Bennett government.

It began by a spread of 2J per cent between the tax on non-residents and the tax on non-resident companies. The spread is now increased to 7\ per cent, and the total tax involved is 22i per cent.
I have this further to say, that a good deal of the assets of these non-resident companies consist of United Kingdom securities. Therefore the companies in Canada, by reason of the exchange control restrictions there, cannot get from England the revenue from their British securities; and yet they are taxed in Canada in respect of that revenue.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
As if
received?

I believe so. Then these companies have very considerable holdings of United States securities, and there they would be subject to the 16i per cent, too. These companies will not have the advantage of non-residents of exemption from the holding tax in respect of dominion government bonds. Putting all these things together cumulatively, we get a result which the traffic

will not bear; in the long run we shall lose this business, and I do not think it will come back.	.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I puzzled over this resolution, and I regret to say that I had not received any illumination on it until I heard the hon. gentleman. What he has stated is extremely disquieting to me. This is going to drive capital out of this country to a degree.
Where is it going to go?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I do not know. It may be liquidated at great loss. It [DOT]seems to me that the minister is endeavouring to put this on a parity, I suppose, with the present taxation on domestic companies.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, on non-residents.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: On nonresidents, all right, but if what the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George has said to-night is correct, I would ask the minister to consider the matter again because I believe it will be a black-eye to foreign capital coming to invest in our securities.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I wish my hon. friend would let me put my side of the matter before him before he passes judgment. I have the greatest respect-it is mutual, my hon. friend says -for the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, but let me tell this story. I cannot go into details because they are extremely complicated, but the Income War Tax Act was amended in 1936 to permit a new species of corporate creature to have existence in this country. They were called non-resident owned investment corporations.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: You found a new victim, that is all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Not at all. These investors were most anxious to come here and incorporate, largely in Charlottetown, to some extent in Montreal and perhaps in some other places in Canada. We provided that they should be taxed at 7i per cent, which was half our corporate rate at the time, but certain deductions were permitted from their income which made the effective rate on these companies five per cent, not 7jt per cent. I said to the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George that I would correct his statement. I should properly have said that I would complete his statement. His statement was perfectly correct, technically, but it was never intended to tax these companies 2i per cent more than non-residents. It was intended to

Income War Tax Act
tax them at the non-resident rate which was five per cent, and this was a way of doing it. The rate in the statute is 7i per cent, but the effective rate on their income was five per cent.
The reason why we are raising this rate, multiplying that original 7J per cent by three, is that we have multiplied the non-resident rate by three. It was five per cent and has now become fifteen per cent, and the effective rate on these companies now is not 22i per cent but, by reason of deductions and adjustments which I cannot describe because they are so complicated but anyone acquainted with them will know what they are, the effective rate is fifteen per cent.
It may be that we shall lose revenue rather than gain revenue by this. I do not know. The resolution is being passed more as a matter of principle than anything else. There was never any undertaking, express or implied, with these corporations that we would not move the rate up if we moved our nonresident rate up. If our non-resident rate goes to fifteen per cent, it is only fair that this rate should also go to fifteen per cent. I do not know whether they will discontinue their corporate existence, but they will in effect be paying only fifteen per cent on the dividends of their shares when they go abroad. Is that not correct?

That applies only to the revenue which was received from dividends of Canadian incorporated companies. On the interest from Canadian bonds the tax will be 22| per cent. I am sure I am correct in that. As a matter of fact, these companies will not benefit from the exemption of section 9 B(2). If they hold the bonds of the Dominion of Canada they will pay 22^ per cent. I know one or two companies which have substantial holdings of Dominion of Canada bonds. They now pay a nine per cent tax on these bonds. Under the proposed amendment they will pay 22i per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman may be right. I was led to believe, and I still believe, that substantially the rate will be fifteen per cent. I will, however, check that.
Only, I think, if the company's entire portfolio is in the shares of Canadian dividend corporations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Do any of these companies hold dominion bonds?
I can speak only of one or two. I have knowledge of their balance sheets, and they are holding almost entirely bonds. There are only two cases I can recall.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What kind of bonds?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I shall have to check the
statements of my hon. friend, but when I was Acting Minister of Finance-I could not get the details of all the various enactments and references from one section to another in my head solidly enough to remember them for more than a day at a time- I remember distinctly that the intention was to give these corporate companies the five per cent rate, and it was considered that by giving them a rate in the act fifty per cent higher, that is the effective rate they would get. It was based upon that, and the theory of this resolution, whether there is some error in detail or not, is that we are giving them the fifteen per cent rate now.

It will not work out in
that way.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
What is
the practice of the department in the application of the law? That would show what the intent was, to a degree at all events. The commissioner of income tax would know.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The practice is to apply
the 7i per cent or the 9 per cent rate as it has been applied since last year. But it is the effect with which we are concerned- what it works out to. We are supposed to arrive at the non-resident rate. These are in effect non-residents. They are individuals. They may have been British who own shares all over the world, property and shares in India, south America, and many other places; they transferred these shares to a Canadian company which, in many instances, had its head office at Charlottetown, and the individual investors took in return the shares of that Canadian company. Then they received dividends on the shares of the company. But for the most part their property

was abroad. They just put that in this for purposes which were advantageous to themselves.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Let me ask a plain question: did they come here to escape taxation in their own jurisdiction? Is that a true statement of affairs? If it is, of course they alienate a certain amount of sympathy which I might have for them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should not like to-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister would not like to say that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I quite appreciate that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should like to ask the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George.

I do not think anyone could give a categorical answer, because, as the minister has said, this has been an exceedingly complicated business. Each company is an individual entity of itself, set up for a special purpose, and usually having a trust behind it. But I would say that many of the companies that were created for the purpose of getting more advantageous taxes have ceased to exist since the change in the British finance act in 1936. For the most part these companies came to Canada to obtain, first, security, and, second, through domiciling themselves in Prince Edward Island they avoided any possibility of double succession duty- which was certainly a substantial advantage. There were, however, other purposes as well.
